Dermatitis herpetiformis, while also pruritic and associated with coeliac disease, presents differently from the rash described here. It typically affects extensor surfaces such as the shins and manifests as vesicular or blistering lesions, unlike the presentation in this case.

Lichen sclerosus
Lichen sclerosus tends to present as pruritic white patches, most commonly affecting the vulva in elderly women, though it can also occur on male genitalia or around the anus. This condition does not produce violaceous lesions and would not typically manifest at the ankles.

Shoe contact dermatitis
Shoe contact dermatitis generally occurs in individuals who wear poorly fitting footwear over prolonged periods or those allergic to materials within their shoes, such as leather. The clinical features differ from those seen in this case; it usually affects both the volar and dorsal aspects of the foot with an erythematous and blistering rash that may be pruritic or painful.

Tinea pedis
Tinea pedis, commonly referred to as athlete's foot, is a fungal infection that predominantly affects interdigital spaces. Its presentation includes dry, scaly white patches and skin cracking—distinctly different from what has been observed in this patient.

stem: A 34-year-old man comes for review. Over the past two weeks he has developed a number of painful, erythematous lesions on his shins. He has no dermatological history of note and is usually fit and well. On examination the lesions are consistent with erythema nodosum. You arrange some baseline investigations. He asks what is likely to happen. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Heal without scarring if steroids are given within 2 weeks
explanation:
Heal without scarring within 1-2 months
The correct answer is Heal without scarring within 1-2 months. Erythema nodosum is a type of panniculitis, an inflammation of the subcutaneous fat. It typically presents as painful, erythematous nodules on the shins and is usually self-limiting. In most cases, the lesions will resolve spontaneously without scarring within 1-2 months.

Heal without scarring if steroids are given within 2 weeks
Although corticosteroids can be used to manage severe or persistent cases of erythema nodosum, they are not necessary for all patients, and their use does not guarantee that healing will occur without scarring. The condition often resolves on its own without treatment.

Heal without scarring within 6-12 months
This option overestimates the duration of healing for erythema nodosum. Most cases resolve much more quickly, usually within 1-2 months.

Heal with scarring within 1-2 months
While it is true that erythema nodosum generally resolves within this timeframe, it typically does so without leaving scars. Scarring is not a common outcome for this condition.

Heal with scarring within 6-12 months
This option both overestimates the duration of healing and incorrectly suggests that scarring is a typical outcome for erythema nodosum. As previously mentioned, the condition usually resolves without scarring in a shorter timeframe (1-2 months).

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with shiny, flat-topped papules on the palmar aspect of the wrists. He is mainly bothered by the troublesome and persistent itching. A diagnosis of lichen planus is suspected. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Topical clobetasone butyrate
The correct answer is Topical clobetasone butyrate. Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the skin, mucous membranes and nails. It presents with flat-topped papules that are often itchy. Topical corticosteroids like clobetasone butyrate are the first-line treatment for cutaneous lichen planus according to UK guidelines. They reduce inflammation and alleviate itching by inhibiting cytokine production and suppressing eosinophil action.

Refer for punch biopsy
Refer for punch biopsy is not the most appropriate initial step in management. While a biopsy can be used to confirm a diagnosis of lichen planus if there's uncertainty, it's typically only performed after an initial trial of treatment or if there's suspicion of malignancy (which would be unusual in this case).

Emollients + oral antihistamine
Emollients + oral antihistamine could provide symptomatic relief from itching but do not address the underlying inflammation causing the symptoms. Emollients moisturise the skin while antihistamines block histamine receptors to reduce itchiness. However, they do not treat the condition itself.

Topical dapsone
Topical dapsone is primarily used for dermatitis herpetiformis and other neutrophilic dermatoses, not lichen planus. Dapsone has anti-inflammatory properties and can be effective against certain skin conditions, but its use should be restricted due to potential side effects including haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

Topical clotrimazole
Topical clotrimazole is an antifungal medication often used to treat conditions such as athlete's foot or thrush. It works by disrupting fungal cell membrane synthesis but has no role in treating lichen planus which is an inflammatory rather than infectious condition.

stem: A 55-year-old woman is referred to the dermatology clinic. She reports a 3-month history of painful oral erosions, followed by the recent appearance of fragile blisters on her trunk. On examination, there are multiple erosions on her buccal mucosa. Several ruptured blisters are noted on her back. Gentle rubbing of the adjacent skin results in separation of the epidermis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Oral prednisolone
Systemic glucocorticoids are the first-line treatment in pemphigus vulgaris. Oral prednisolone is the correct answer. The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune blistering disease. Key features in this case include the initial and prominent mucosal involvement (painful oral erosions), followed by the development of fragile, easily ruptured skin blisters. The positive Nikolsky's sign (separation of the epidermis on gentle rubbing) is a classic finding. Pemphigus vulgaris is a serious and potentially fatal condition, and the primary goal of initial treatment is to rapidly suppress autoantibody production and inflammation to halt the formation of new blisters. High-dose systemic glucocorticoids, such as oral prednisolone, are the cornerstone and first-line therapy to achieve rapid disease control.

Topical clobetasol propionate
Topical clobetasol propionate is a very potent topical steroid. While useful for localised inflammatory or blistering skin conditions (such as limited bullous pemphigoid), it would be inadequate to control the widespread mucocutaneous disease seen in this patient with pemphigus vulgaris. Systemic therapy is required to manage the underlying autoimmune process.

Oral azathioprine
Oral azathioprine is an immunosuppressive agent frequently used in the management of pemphigus vulgaris. However, it is used as a 'steroidsparing' agent to allow for the dose of prednisolone to be reduced and to maintain long-term remission. Its onset of action is slow (typically 6-8 weeks), making it unsuitable for inducing rapid remission as a first-line monotherapy. It is usually initiated concurrently with systemic steroids.

Oral dapsone
Oral dapsone is the first-line treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis, another autoimmune blistering disease. However, the clinical features are different; dermatitis herpetiformis is characterised by intensely pruritic (itchy) vesicles, typically on extensor surfaces like the elbows and knees, and is strongly associated with coeliac disease. The presentation of painful oral erosions and flaccid, non-pruritic bullae is not typical for dermatitis herpetiformis.

Rituximab infusion
Rituximab infusion is a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20-positive B-cells and is a highly effective therapy for pemphigus vulgaris. It is increasingly used in severe or refractory cases, and some guidelines now suggest its use first-line in combination with steroids. However, for the purposes of postgraduate exams, high-dose systemic steroids remain the standard initial therapy to gain rapid control, with other agents like rituximab often introduced for refractory disease or as a primary steroidsparing strategy.

stem: A 47-year-old lorry driver presents following the development of a widespread urticarial rash. This is associated with pruritus. What is the most appropriate medication to help relieve the itch?
explanation:
Loratadine
The obvious concern in a lorry driver is drowsiness. Of the non-sedating antihistamines, there is some evidence that loratadine causes less drowsiness than cetirizine.

Cetirizine
The obvious concern in a lorry driver is drowsiness. Of the non-sedating antihistamines, there is some evidence that cetirizine causes more drowsiness than loratadine.

Chlorphenamine
Chlorphenamine is a sedating antihistamine and would not be appropriate for a lorry driver due to the risk of drowsiness.

Ranitidine
Ranitidine is an H2 receptor antagonist and is not used for the treatment of urticaria or pruritus.

Alimemazine
Alimemazine is a sedating antihistamine and would not be appropriate for a lorry driver due to the risk of drowsiness.

stem: A 40-year-old woman who has suffered from severe lupus nephritis in the past necessitating a renal transplant from her husband, who acted as the donor, presents to dermatology clinic with a mole on her back. She states her husband noticed the mole at the end of their cruise around the world, which they went on earlier this year. It has been itchy and bleeding recently. The transplant was a success and 7 years later she is still taking tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisolone, lansoprazole, Adcal D3, aspirin and atorvastatin. Over the last 7 years she has been admitted to hospital with a few episodes of pneumonia which cleared with antibiotics and a self-resolving episode of presumed lupus pericarditis. On examination: an 8mm, firm, pink and brown slightly raised lesion with a crusted surface and an irregular border. This was located on the skin overlying the right scapula. What is the most likely diagnosis of this lesion?
explanation:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
Squamous cell carcinoma is the correct option, given the typical appearance, the UV exposure described above and the fact that SCC is the most common malignancy secondary to immunosuppression.

Actinic keratoses
Actinic keratoses is incorrect as these are typically dry, scaly patches caused by years of skin exposure and can develop into SCC if left untreated.

Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)
BCC is incorrect as BCC typically presents as a 'rodents ulcer' with a rolled edge not seen here, and is less common than SCC with the background of immunosuppression described here.

Bowen's Disease
Bowen's disease is incorrect as this disease describes the slow growing pre-malignant form of SCC and may appear like above, but is most common in elderly women and the immunosuppression aspect makes SCC more likely.

Malignant Melanoma
Malignant melanoma is incorrect. Even though the lesion above could be a melanoma as transplant recipients are more likely to have this compared to the general population; however SCC is a more likely option.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents due to the development of 'hard skin' on his scalp. On examination he has a 9cm circular, white, hyperkeratotic lesion on the crown of his head. He has no past history of any skin or scalp disorder. Skin scrapings are reported as follows: No fungal elements seen What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Psoriasis
As the skin scraping is negative for fungi the most likely diagnosis is psoriasis. Scalp psoriasis may occur in isolation in patients with no history of psoriasis elsewhere. Please see the link for more information. The white appearance of the lesion is secondary to the 'silver scale' covering the psoriatic plaque.

stem: A 68-year-old female presents with a 5-month history of itching near her buttocks. On examination, there is an excoriated depigmented patch measuring 3x4cm, located around 2cm lateral to the anus on the right side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen sclerosus
Lichen sclerosus: itchy white spots typically seen on the vulva of elderly women. The excoriation simply points to the patch being itchy (and therefore the patient scratching it, causing excoriation). White patches are typical of lichen sclerosus, which often occurs near the genital area. Exam questions will often involve an elderly female and the lesion appearing on the vulva. However, it is important to note that it may happen in other areas, such as the thighs and anal region. In males, it usually affects the glans penis, in which case it is called balanitis xerotica obliterans.

Herpes simplex virus
Herpes simplex would present with clusters of inflamed papules and vesicles and not with a single white patch. It would also be painful, rather than only itchy.

Vitiligo
Vitiligo is a reasonable differential as there is a depigmented patch. Patchy loss of skin color, which usually first appears on the hands, face, and areas around body openings and the genitals is characteristic of vitiligo. Although it may appear at any time from birth to senescence, onset is most commonly observed in persons aged 10-30 years with an average age of onset of 20 years. It is not typically so itchy as to cause notable excoriation, unlike lichen. For these reasons it is not the most likely diagnosis.

Candidiasis
Candidiasis (thrush) would present with cottage cheese-like discharge and itching and does not typically present with a single white patch, though oral thrush may present with a white patch on the tongue that can be scraped off.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis would present with a well-demarcated erythematous patch covered with a silvery scale. It is unlikely to present for the first time in a patient this age and in this area.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has been referred to the dermatology clinic with a 4-week history of skin rash. Past medical history includes mild asthma. Regular medications include folic acid 400micrograms OD and over-the-counter vitamin supplements due to pregnancy. She feels well in herself but states she had a mild cold when the lesions first developed. On examination, she has multiple, discrete, raised erythematous lesions on the arms and legs ranging from 8cm in diameter to 12cm in diameter. There is pain on active and passive joint movement. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum may be caused by pregnancy. The above scenario holds multiple crucial pieces of information that combined give the correct answer of erythema nodosum. Erythema nodosum typically lasts for 4-6 weeks, can develop after a flu-like illness, is associated with multiple erythematous lesions affecting the limbs, and is associated with pregnancy. Lesions are often nodular and tender, and the rash is self-terminating. It is often accompanied by arthralgia.

Erythema ab igne
Erythema ab igne is a reticulated rash caused by over-exposure to infrared radiation. It commonly occurs in people with high levels of exposure to heat such as fireplaces and hot water bottles. It is not associated with recent illness and there are no discrete lesions.

Erythema marginatum
Erythema marginatum is a skin rash that commonly affects the limbs. However, the lesions are typically circular with a raised outer area and pale center and also affect the torso. It is associated with multiple conditions, most commonly rheumatic fever and group A Streptococcus. It is not associated with pregnancy.

Erythema migrans
Erythema migrans is the classic Lyme disease rash appearing in 80% of Lyme disease cases. It appears as a 'bull's eye' rash with a red outer circle, pale inner circle, and red center.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme rash initially appears as red patches on the hands before progressing to target lesions. It is associated with many infections including bacterial, viral, and fungal, and is thought to be an immune-mediated reaction.

stem: A 23-year-old man with very severe Crohn's disease has been put on complete bowel rest for an indefinite period of time whilst he continues his in-patient recovery. He has been receiving total parenteral nutrition for the past few weeks. Recently he has noticed his skin becoming dry and scaly with mouth ulcers and lip swelling. What is the likely cause of these changes?
explanation:
Zinc deficiency
Zinc deficiency caused by total parenteral nutrition (TPN) can result in acrodermatitis herpetiformis. Various small bowel diseases that cause destruction or malfunction of the gut mucosa and malabsorption lead to zinc deficiency. This has similarly been noticed in patients on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) who do not receive zinc - resulting in acrodermatitis herpetiformis causing peri-orificial dermatitis and alopecia.

Selenium deficiency
Selenium deficiency can contribute to fatigue, hair loss, weight gain, joint and muscle pain.

Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency can contribute to fatigue, weakness, pale skin, chest pain, shortness of breath, headache, dizziness and cold peripheries.

Vitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause a smooth tongue, nerve problems like numbness or tingling, pale skin and weakness.

Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency can cause a lack of energy, pale skin, palpitations, headaches and loss of appetite.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to his GP with a long-standing red, scaly rash mainly affecting the scalp, periorbital, auricular and nasolabial folds. The rash is itchy and the skin appears red and inflamed. A diagnosis of seborrheic dermatitis is suspected and the patient was prescribed several topical agents with a plan to follow up with a dermatologist if no improvement is achieved. What chronic condition is most associated with this patient's skin condition?
explanation:
HIV
HIV is associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis. Seborrheic dermatitis, which is believed to be due to several factors including an inflammatory response to the fungus Malassezia furfur, commonly affects areas of the body high in oil-producing glands such as the scalp, face and chest. Although the condition affects approximately 2-5% of the general population, it is significantly associated with immunocompromise and can affect 85-95% of patients with HIV. Although the exact mechanism is not fully understood, it is likely that immunocompromised patients are at increased risk due to the overgrowth of the Malassezia yeast.

Chronic kidney disease
Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly end-stage renal disease, can develop a pruritic, dry rash often referred to as 'renal rash'. It is believed to be secondary to increased serum levels of substances normally filtered by the kidneys such as urea. Although some patients with CKD are immunocompromised and therefore are at potentially higher risk of seborrheic dermatitis, a clear association between the conditions has not been established.

Eczema
The cause of eczema is multifactorial and believed to be due to a combination of genetic and environmental stimuli promoting inflammation of the skin. It is a separate condition from seborrheic dermatitis and there is no clear association between the two.

Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is commonly associated with thinning of the skin and Grave's disease, the commonest cause of hyperthyroidism, can cause a condition known as pretibial myxoedema seen as a waxy, discoloured induration of the skin (normally of the lower legs). Seborrheic dermatitis is however not associated with hyperthyroidism.

Sarcoidosis
The skin is the second-most affected body organ in sarcoidosis after the lungs. Sarcoidosis is associated with diagnoses including erythema nodosum, subcutaneous nodules, and lupus pernio. Seborrheic dermatitis is however not associated with sarcoidosis.

stem: A 34-year-old patient who is known to have psoriasis presents with erythematous skin in the groin and genital area. He also has erythematous skin in the axilla. In the past he has expressed a dislike of messy or cumbersome creams. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Topical steroid
Flexural psoriasis - topical steroid This patient has flexural psoriasis which responds well to topical steroids.

Coal tar
Mild tar preparations are an option but may be messy and cumbersome.

Topical calcipotriol
Topical calcipotriol is usually irritant in flexures.

stem: A 62-year-old with a history of acne rosacea presents for advice regarding treatment. Which one of the following interventions has the least role in management?
explanation:
Low-dose topical corticosteroids
The correct answer is low-dose topical corticosteroids. In the management of acne rosacea, the use of low-dose topical corticosteroids is generally not recommended. This is because their long-term use can exacerbate rosacea, leading to steroid-induced rosacea or rosacea-like dermatitis. Furthermore, abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use can lead to a flare-up of symptoms.

Camouflage creams
Camouflage creams can be beneficial in managing acne rosacea. They are particularly useful for patients who are self-conscious about the redness and flushing associated with the condition. These creams have a green tint that neutralises redness and can improve patients' confidence and quality of life.

Topical metronidazole
Topical metronidazole plays a crucial role in the management of acne rosacea. According to NICE guidelines, it is one of the first-line treatments for this condition due to its anti-inflammatory properties.

Laser therapy
Laser therapy, specifically vascular laser or intense pulsed light treatment, is an effective intervention for reducing persistent redness and visible blood vessels (telangiectasia) associated with rosacea. It may not be first-line due to cost and availability but has a definite role in management.

Use of high-factor sun block
Use of high-factor sun block is recommended as part of general skincare advice for patients with acne rosacea. Sun exposure can worsen symptoms so protecting skin from UV light forms part an important part of disease management.

stem: A 29-year-old man consults you regarding a rash he has noticed around his groin. It has been present for the past 3 months and is asymptomatic. On examination, a symmetrical rash around the groin is noted consisting of well-defined pink/brown patches with fine scaling and superficial fissures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythrasma
The most likely diagnosis in this case is Erythrasma. Erythrasma is a superficial skin infection caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium minutissimum. It typically presents as well-defined, pink or brown patches with fine scaling and superficial fissures in intertriginous areas such as the groin, axillae, and inframammary folds. The condition is often asymptomatic and can be confirmed by observing coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp examination due to the presence of porphyrins produced by the bacteria.

Pityriasis versicolor
Pityriasis versicolor is an incorrect option because it is a superficial fungal infection caused by Malassezia species. It presents as hypo- or hyperpigmented macules with fine scaling, commonly on the trunk and upper extremities. The distribution of the rash and its appearance do not match the description in this case.

Secondary syphilis
Secondary syphilis is also an incorrect choice. Although secondary syphilis may present with a rash that can involve the groin area, it typically manifests as coppery red, non-pruritic maculopapular lesions that involve other areas of the body such as palms and soles. Additionally, secondary syphilis would usually present with accompanying systemic symptoms like fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy.

Acanthosis nigricans
Acanthosis nigricans can be ruled out because it presents as velvety, hyperpigmented plaques commonly affecting areas like neck folds, axillae or knuckles rather than symmetrical patches around the groin. Acanthosis nigricans is often associated with insulin resistance or obesity.

Candida intertrigo
Candida intertrigo is not the most likely diagnosis because although it can affect intertriginous areas like the groin, it usually presents as erythematous, macerated plaques with satellite pustules and is often associated with pruritus. The description of well-defined pink/brown patches with fine scaling and superficial fissures does not fit the typical presentation of Candida intertrigo.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of seborrhoeic dermatitis presents in late winter due a flare in his symptoms, affecting both his face and scalp. Which one of the following agents is least likely to be beneficial?
explanation:
Aqueous cream
The correct answer is aqueous cream, as this is the least likely agent to be beneficial in seborrhoeic dermatitis. Aqueous cream is a simple emollient that lacks any specific anti-inflammatory or antifungal properties necessary for treating seborrhoeic dermatitis. In fact, aqueous cream can sometimes act as an irritant due to its sodium lauryl sulfate content, potentially exacerbating the condition.

Topical ketoconazole
Topical ketoconazole is an effective treatment for seborrhoeic dermatitis as it has both antifungal and anti-inflammatory properties. It targets Malassezia species, which are believed to play a key role in the pathogenesis of seborrhoeic dermatitis. It is available as both cream and shampoo formulations and is considered a first-line treatment.

Selenium sulphide shampoo
Selenium sulphide shampoo is beneficial due to its antifungal and keratolytic properties. It helps reduce scaling and controls the growth of Malassezia yeasts. It is particularly useful for scalp involvement and can be used as maintenance therapy to prevent recurrences.

Topical hydrocortisone
Topical hydrocortisone is valuable in managing seborrhoeic dermatitis due to its anti-inflammatory properties. As a mild topical corticosteroid, it helps reduce inflammation, redness, and itching associated with the condition. It is particularly useful during acute flares but should be used judiciously due to potential side effects with prolonged use.

Tar shampoo
Tar shampoo is beneficial due to its antiproliferative and antiinflammatory properties. It helps reduce scaling and inflammation, particularly in scalp involvement. Coal tar preparations can be used alongside other treatments and are particularly useful for maintenance therapy.

stem: A 29-year-old male has noticed some rashes developing on his body over the last 2 weeks. They are present on his forearms and his calves and are reported as quite itchy. On examination the rashes are erythematous large plaques with a silvery surface on the flexor aspects of the upper and lower limbs. The plaques are Auspitz's sign positive. What is the first-line management for this condition?
options: Topical steroids and vitamin D analogues
explanation:
Topical steroids
Topical steroids is correct (see below) as the first-line NICE recommendation for treatment of flexural psoriasis. Mild to moderate topical steroids are prescribed for no longer than 2 weeks at a time.

Coal tar preparations
Coal tar preparations are incorrect as this is the third-line NICE recommendation for chronic plaque psoriasis.

Tacrolimus ointment
Tacrolimus ointment is incorrect as this is a second-line option for treatment of face, scalp, flexural or genital psoriasis.

Topical steroids and vitamin D analogues
Topical steroids and vitamin D analogues are incorrect as this combination is the first-line NICE recommendation for chronic plaque psoriasis.

Vitamin D analogues
Vitamin D analogues are incorrect as this is a second-line option for treatment of face, scalp, flexural or genital psoriasis.

stem: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with a persistent skin rash on his hands, arms, neck and face. The rash is red-brown in colour, symmetrical and scaly. He also complains of a poor appetite, nausea and diarrhoea. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely to have caused his symptoms?
explanation:
Niacin
Niacin (B3) deficiency is characterised by dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, a condition known as pellagra. The patient's symptoms of a red-brown, symmetrical, scaly rash on the skin, poor appetite, nausea and diarrhoea are characteristic of pellagra, which is caused by a deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3). Niacin plays a crucial role in cellular metabolism and energy production. Chronic alcoholism can lead to malnutrition and poor absorption of essential vitamins and minerals, including niacin.

Folic acid
Folic acid deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia with symptoms such as fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath and glossitis (inflammation of the tongue). Although alcoholics are at risk for folic acid deficiency due to malnutrition and poor absorption, the patient's symptoms do not fit this diagnosis.

Thiamine
A deficiency in Thiamine (vitamin B1) can result in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome or beriberi. Symptoms include peripheral neuropathy, muscle weakness, confusion, memory loss and ophthalmoplegia. While chronic alcoholism is a common cause of thiamine deficiency, the patient's presentation does not match these conditions.

Vitamin B6
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency may cause peripheral neuropathy, irritability and depression. However, these symptoms are not consistent with the patient's presentation.

Zinc
Zinc deficiency can lead to dermatitis (skin inflammation), hair loss and immune dysfunction but does not fully explain the specific rash pattern described in this case.

stem: A 54-year-old Caucasian man presents with a rash on the face. He first noticed this four months ago when he experienced episodes of flushing on the face. This has often occurred after he had alcohol or in situations where he felt stressful. A month ago, he started noticing a rash on his cheeks which came on intermittently until two weeks ago when the rash has become permanent. There has been no pain or itch associated with the rash. He is otherwise fit and well. He does not smoke. On examination of the face, there is marked erythema with papules, pustules and telangiectasia. There are no comedones seen. The rash is distributed across the cheeks and nose. There is no per-oral or periorbital involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acne rosacea
Rosacea features: nose, cheeks and forehead flushing, erythema, telangiectasia → papules and pustules. Acne rosacea is the best fit for this patient because the clinical picture combines several cardinal features: episodic flushing precipitated by alcohol and emotional stress, fixed central facial erythema with telangiectasia, and later development of papules and pustules in the absence of comedones. These appearances, along with the typical anatomical distribution over the cheeks and nose, are classic for rosacea.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus can present with a malar or ‘butterfly’ rash but it is usually macular, non-scarring and photosensitive, and crucially spares the nasolabial folds. Papules, pustules and telangiectasia are uncommon in acute cutaneous lupus. Moreover, the patient has no systemic features such as arthralgia or constitutional upset, making SLE less likely.

Acne vulgaris
Acne vulgaris typically shows open and closed comedones as the first lesions, followed by inflammatory papules, pustules and nodules. Comedones are notably absent in this scenario, and adult-onset inflammatory acne without comedones is unusual. In addition, flushing episodes are not characteristic of acne vulgaris.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Seborrhoeic dermatitis affects seborrhoeic areas – scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds and retro-auricular skin – and manifests as greasy, yellowish, scaling erythema rather than discrete papules and pustules. Telangiectasia and flushing are not prominent features, so the description does not correspond with seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Perioral dermatitis
Perioral dermatitis presents with clusters of tiny papulopustules around the mouth, occasionally the peri-ocular skin, and typically spares a clear rim next to the vermilion border. In this patient, the eruption is centred on the cheeks and nose with no perioral involvement, making this diagnosis improbable. Unlike rosacea, perioral dermatitis is often associated with the use of topical corticosteroids, which is not mentioned here.

stem: A 40-year-old man with known end-stage renal failure has been on peritoneal dialysis for the past 5 years. Family screening for a possible donor identified a potential match with his brother and following appropriate counselling a successful renal transplant was performed. On his 3-monthly review, there is no evidence of graft rejection. What malignancy is this patient most at risk of in the future?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
Renal transplant patients - skin cancer (particularly squamous cell) is the most common malignancy secondary to immunosuppression. All patients who undergo renal transplantation must be commenced and remain on immunosuppression therapy for the rest of their life to prevent the risk of transplant rejection. As an adverse effect, this immunosuppression therapy results in patients having an increased risk of carcinomas as their immune system is less able to identify and destroy newly formed cancer cells or prevent infections that may cause cancer. Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin has been shown to be the most common malignancy associated with immunosuppression.

Adenocarcinoma of the bowel
Adenocarcinoma of the bowel is the commonest form of colorectal cancer. Although its incidence, like most cancers, is increased in immunosuppressed patients there are several other risks factor associated with this cancer including dietary imbalances, smoking and a lack of physical exercise. As such colorectal cancer is less common in immunosuppressed patients when compared to other cancers.

Adenocarcinoma of the prostate
Adenocarcinoma of the prostate is mainly associated with obesity, hypertension and elevated testosterone levels. There is an increased risk of this form of cancer in immunosuppressed patients however it is not the commonest associated cancer.

B-cell lymphoma
B-cell lymphoma is the group of blood and lymph tumours that develop from the B lymphocytes including both Hodgkin's and most non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Although there is an increased risk of lymphoma in patients on immunosuppression their incidence remains low.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
The association between immunosuppression and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is not fully understood and although an increased risk may exist, the incidence of CLL in these patients is lower than other cancers.

stem: Which of the following skin conditions associated with malignancy are not correctly paired?
explanation:
Erythema gyratum repens and lymphoma
Erythema gyratum repens is a paraneoplastic eruption with a 'woodgrain' pattern and figurate erythema commonly seen in patients with lung cancer. Erythema gyratum repens is generally associated with solid organ malignancies such as lung and breast cancer.

stem: An 82-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic with a 3-week history of intensely pruritic, tense bullae on his trunk and flexural surfaces. Examination reveals widespread erythematous plaques with overlying large, fluid-filled blisters. The oral mucosa is spared. A perilesional skin biopsy is taken for direct immunofluorescence. What is the most likely finding?
options: Granular IgA deposition in dermal papillae
Linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction
Subepidermal blister with a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate
explanation:
Linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction
Linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction is the correct answer. The clinical presentation of an elderly patient with intensely pruritic, tense bullae on flexural surfaces, with sparing of the oral mucosa, is classic for bullous pemphigoid. This is an autoimmune blistering disease caused by antibodies (predominantly IgG) targeting hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230) in the basement membrane zone. Direct immunofluorescence of a perilesional skin biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis, revealing a characteristic linear deposition of IgG and/or C3 along the dermoepidermal junction.

Granular IgA deposition in dermal papillae
Granular IgA deposition in dermal papillae is the pathognomonic finding in dermatitis herpetiformis. This condition typically presents with intensely itchy, symmetrical vesicles on extensor surfaces (e.g., elbows, knees, buttocks) and is strongly associated with coeliac disease. The clinical picture in this scenario, with large tense bullae, is not typical for dermatitis herpetiformis.

Intraepidermal IgG deposition
Intraepidermal IgG deposition is the characteristic immunofluorescence finding in pemphigus vulgaris. While also an autoimmune blistering disease, pemphigus vulgaris is distinguished by flaccid, easily ruptured bullae and frequent, often severe, mucosal involvement. The patient's tense bullae and spared mucosa make this diagnosis less likely.

Subepidermal blister with a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate
Subepidermal blister with a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate describes a histological finding, not an immunofluorescence pattern. While a subepidermal split is seen in bullous pemphigoid, the infiltrate is typically rich in eosinophils. A predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate would be more suggestive of conditions like dermatitis herpetiformis or linear IgA bullous dermatosis.

Epidermal hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis
Epidermal hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis are histological features characteristic of psoriasis. Psoriasis is a papulosquamous disorder and does not typically present with large bullae, although it can be pruritic. This finding would not be expected in a primary autoimmune blistering disease.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation has a pruritic rash on her lower abdomen. She reports it initially appeared as small, pink spots over her stretch marks, but has since spread to her thighs. She has gestational diabetes and worries this rash is similar to the chickenpox she had as a child. On examination, she has multiple erythematous plaques over her lower abdomen, sparing the periumbilical region. There is no blistering or mucosal involvement. Which option is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP) is correct. PEP most commonly occurs in the third trimester and is characterised by pruritic papules and plaques that initially arise within abdominal striae, sparing the periumbilical region. The rash can then spread to the buttocks and thighs and does not usually affect the face. The absence of blistering or mucosal involvement further supports PEP over other dermatoses.

Atopic eruption of pregnancy
Atopic eruption of pregnancy (AEP) is incorrect. While AEP can also cause pruritic skin lesions during pregnancy, lesions tend to appear during the first or second trimester and tend to affect sites commonly affected in eczema (e.g. flexures) rather than the abdomen initially. The evolution of pruritic papules to erythematous plaques is also more in keeping with PEP.

Herpes zoster infection
Herpes zoster infection is incorrect. While this can cause a pruritic rash, the rash is often painful, localised to a dermatome, and characterised by lesions that evolve from macules and papules to vesicles, which become pustular and crust over. This patient has no blistering and her rash does not follow a specific dermatome.

Pemphigoid gestationis
Pemphigoid gestationis is incorrect. While PG can also develop in the second or third trimester with pruritic abdominal skin lesions, it typically begins as urticarial papules and plaques that become tense blisters, which is not seen here. In PG, umbilical involvement is common, unlike in this patient who has umbilical sparing.

Varicella zoster infection
Varicella zoster infection is incorrect. While this pathogen causes chickenpox, which can cause pruritic skin lesions, it is characterised by lesions that progress from macules to papules to vesicles, which then crust over. Additionally, the rash is widespread, affecting the face, trunk, and extremities, often involving the mucous membranes, and does not typically spare the umbilicus or localise to stretch marks.

stem: A 73-year-old woman is seen by the dermatologist with a mole on her back. It measures 8mm in diameter, has irregular borders and is noted to have variation in colour. A biopsy taken confirms malignant melanoma with an invasive depth of 4mm, there is also ulceration present. The tumour is shown to carry a BRAF mutation and has a high mitotic rate. She has asked if she is likely to die from the illness. Which is the worst prognostic factor in this case?
explanation:
Depth of the lesion
The invasion depth of the tumour is the single most important prognostic factor. The most important factor in determining prognosis in malignant melanoma is Breslow thickness, which is an indicator of the invasive depth of the tumour. 4mm represents a large thickness and is the most important poor prognosticator for this patient.

BRAF mutation
BRAF mutation is seen in 50% of malignant melanomas. Although it is not directly linked to a worse prognosis, its presence permits the use of the BRAF inhibitor, vemurafenib, which improves survival in late-stage disease.

Diameter of the lesion
8mm diameter is a red flag when assessing lesions using the 'ABCDEs' of melanoma, and although a large diameter increases the likelihood of increased invasive depth, prognostically it is not as important as the thickness of the lesion.

Mitotic rate
A high mitotic rate is a poor prognostic marker but is the second-most predictor of mortality after the invasive depth of a lesion.

Ulceration
Ulceration of the lesion is a poor prognostic marker, however, it is not as closely linked to mortality as invasive depth.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, currently 14 weeks pregnant, presents to her GP with worsening acne. On examination, she has widespread non-inflammatory lesions, numerous papules and pustules, and extensive inflammatory lesions, some of which are nodules. She is concerned about the potential for pitting and scarring. What medication should be commenced alongside topical benzoyl peroxide?
explanation:
Oral erythromycin
Oral erythromycin is the correct choice for this patient presenting with features in keeping with moderate to severe acne vulgaris. Erythromycin is a safe antibiotic option that effectively reduces bacterial proliferation and inflammation in acne. Given the patient is pregnant, erythromycin is preferred because it does not pose significant risks to the developing foetus, unlike other medications such as isotretinoin or tetracyclines. Thus, combining oral erythromycin with topical benzoyl peroxide provides a suitable treatment approach for her acne while prioritising maternal and foetal safety.

Oral isotretinoin
Oral isotretinoin is incorrect in this case because it is highly teratogenic and poses significant risks to a developing foetus, particularly in the first trimester. Its use is contraindicated in pregnancy due to the potential for severe birth defects and other complications.

Oral minocycline
Oral minocycline is incorrect as it belongs to the tetracycline class of antibiotics, which is contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of adverse effects on the foetus. Tetracyclines can cause teeth discolouration and affect bone growth in the developing baby.

Topical dapsone
Topical dapsone is incorrect for this case because, while it is generally considered safe for use during pregnancy, it is less effective for treating moderate to severe acne compared to other available options. Dapsone primarily targets inflammatory lesions but may not adequately address the widespread non-inflammatory lesions and papules described in this patient. Additionally, its efficacy in pregnancy has not been as well established as that of oral erythromycin, making it a less suitable choice for this situation.

Topical tazarotene
Topical tazarotene is incorrect because it is a potent retinoid that is contraindicated during pregnancy due to its potential teratogenic effects. The use of tazarotene can lead to serious risks for the developing foetus, including birth defects. Although it is effective for treating acne vulgaris by promoting cell turnover and reducing lesions, its safety profile makes it unsuitable for pregnant women, highlighting the need for safer alternatives like oral erythromycin in this context.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the general practice by his mother, reporting a sudden onset of a rash on his arms, chest, and around his mouth. On examination, you observe multiple monomorphic papulovesicular lesions with punched-out erosions, each approximately 1-2mm in diameter, accompanied by crusting over the lesions. The child has a history of eczema and recently commenced nursery school. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Eczema herpeticum
Eczema herpeticum rash can be described as monomorphic punched-out erosions (circular, depressed, ulcerated lesions) usually 1-3 mm in diameter. The most likely diagnosis is eczema herpeticum. This condition is a severe primary infection of the skin by herpes simplex virus 1 or 2, often seen in children with atopic eczema. The child's presentation of monomorphic papulovesicular lesions with punched-out erosions, each approximately 1-2mm in diameter, accompanied by crusting over the lesions is consistent with this diagnosis. Additionally, the sudden onset of the rash and his history of eczema further support this diagnosis.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is characterised by the appearance of target lesions on the palms and soles, which subsequently spread to the torso and limbs. This is not described in this case.

Impetigo
Impetigo is recognised by its hallmark golden-crusted lesions, frequently located around the mouth. Although this case describes crusting, it is not golden, and the other features are more consistent with eczema herpeticum.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome predominantly affects infants and presents with a severe desquamating rash that progresses to form superficial fluid-filled blisters. This is not described in this case.

Varicella zoster virus
Varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox) manifests initially as an erythematous maculopapular rash, which evolves into vesicles filled with clear fluid. This is not described in this case.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with blistering lesions on her leg is diagnosed as having bullous pemphigoid. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Oral corticosteroids
Oral corticosteroids is the correct answer for the initial management of bullous pemphigoid in this 65-year-old woman. Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disorder characterised by the formation of tense bullae on the skin, commonly affecting the elderly. The condition results from autoantibodies targeting components of the basement membrane zone, specifically BP180 and BP230, leading to separation at the dermal-epidermal junction. Oral corticosteroids, typically prednisolone at a dose of 0.5-1 mg/kg/day, are the first-line systemic therapy for moderate to severe bullous pemphigoid. They effectively suppress the inflammatory response and autoantibody production, leading to rapid disease control. The dose is gradually tapered once disease control is achieved, with the aim of finding the minimum effective maintenance dose to prevent relapse whilst minimising side effects.

Reassurance
Reassurance alone is inappropriate for bullous pemphigoid. This is a serious autoimmune condition that can cause significant morbidity if left untreated. The blisters can be painful, prone to infection, and may lead to extensive skin erosions. Without proper treatment, the disease typically follows a chronic course with periods of remission and exacerbation. Reassurance without active treatment would allow the disease to progress, potentially leading to complications such as secondary infection, scarring, and significant impact on quality of life.

Topical corticosteroids
Topical corticosteroids may be used in mild, localised disease or as adjunctive therapy to systemic treatment. High-potency topical corticosteroids (such as clobetasol propionate) can be effective for limited disease. However, in a patient presenting with established blistering lesions, particularly if widespread, topical therapy alone is usually insufficient as initial management. Topical treatments may be considered as the disease comes under control or for maintenance therapy, but they are not typically the first-line approach for moderate to severe disease.

Oral itraconazole
Oral itraconazole is an antifungal medication with no role in the management of bullous pemphigoid. This medication targets fungal cell membranes and would not address the autoimmune pathophysiology of bullous pemphigoid. Itraconazole would be appropriate for fungal infections such as dermatophytosis, onychomycosis, or systemic mycoses, but has no efficacy in autoimmune blistering disorders. Using itraconazole would delay appropriate treatment and allow the bullous pemphigoid to progress.

Screen for solid-tumour malignancies
Screen for solid-tumour malignancies is not the most appropriate initial management step, although there is a modest association between bullous pemphigoid and malignancy. While some studies suggest a slightly increased risk of certain malignancies in patients with bullous pemphigoid, the association is not strong enough to warrant routine screening beyond age-appropriate cancer screening. The priority in this case is to initiate treatment to control the active skin disease. Any cancer screening should follow standard age-appropriate guidelines and be based on individual risk factors rather than being triggered by the diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid alone.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant presents to the antenatal clinic with a worsening rash on her legs. She had initially noticed multiple small red rounded lumps on both her lower legs. The lesions initially measured 3cm in diameter and have been slowly growing in size over the past two weeks. The lesions now range between 6-9cm nodules on both her shins which were becoming painful. This is her second pregnancy and she denied experiencing a similar rash before. What is the likely cause for the rash in this case?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum may be caused by pregnancy. Erythema nodosum is a condition that causes painful red bumps under the skin on the shins. It is one of the most common forms of panniculitis that causes inflammation of the subcutaneous fat under the skin. It can occur in pregnancy due to hormonal changes.

Erythema ab igne
Erythema ab igne is a skin reaction caused by chronic exposure to infrared radiation in the form of heat and is not commonly seen as a direct result of pregnancy.

Erythema gyratum repens
Erythema gyratum repens is a rare paraneoplastic type of annular erythema with a distinctive figurate 'wood-grain' appearance. It has a strong association with malignancy.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction usually triggered by infections, most commonly herpes simplex virus (HSV) and can be associated with pregnancy. However, it appears as target-like patches (dark circles with purple-grey centres) which are not described here.

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is a relatively common skin disorder that can occur in women during pregnancy. It usually presents within the first pregnancy. It appears as an itchy, bumpy rash that starts in the stretch marks of the abdomen in the last 3 months of pregnancy then clears with delivery. This is unlikely to be the case here.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to the dermatology clinic with a 2-year history of intermittent flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea. On examination, she has multiple reddish-brown macules on her trunk, which she notes become raised and itchy when rubbed. Her full blood count is shown. Hb 125 g/L (115 - 160) Platelets 240 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 9.8 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Monocytes 1.2 * 109/L (0.2 - 1.0) What is the most appropriate initial investigation to support the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Serum tryptase
Serum tryptase is the first-line investigation in suspected systemic mastocytosis. The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of systemic mastocytosis. The combination of systemic symptoms (flushing, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea) and cutaneous findings is classic. The reddish-brown macules that become raised and itchy upon rubbing describe urticaria pigmentosa with a positive Darier's sign, which is pathognomonic for mastocytosis. The mild monocytosis is also a recognised haematological association. The next step is to investigate for evidence of systemic mast cell activation or proliferation. Serum tryptase is the correct answer. Tryptase is a neutral protease that is highly concentrated in the secretory granules of mast cells. A persistently elevated baseline serum tryptase level (>20 ng/mL) is a minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis according to the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria. It is the recommended firstline, minimally invasive investigation when there is a clinical suspicion of this condition. It serves as an excellent screening tool to assess the total body mast cell load. If elevated, it would provide strong evidence for the diagnosis and justify proceeding to more definitive and invasive investigations, such as a bone marrow biopsy.

Bone marrow biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy is the gold standard for the definitive diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis. It allows for histological examination to identify multifocal, dense infiltrates of mast cells, and for ancillary testing such as immunohistochemistry (for tryptase, KIT) and molecular analysis for the characteristic KIT D816V mutation. However, it is an invasive procedure and is not the appropriate initial investigation. It is reserved for patients in whom less invasive tests, such as serum tryptase, are positive or where there is a very high clinical suspicion despite normal tryptase levels.

Skin biopsy
Skin biopsy of one of the macules would likely confirm the diagnosis of urticaria pigmentosa by demonstrating an increased number of mast cells in the dermis. While this would confirm cutaneous mastocytosis, it would not assess the systemic component of the disease, which is suggested by the patient's flushing, abdominal symptoms, and monocytosis. Serum tryptase is a better initial test to evaluate for systemic involvement, which is the key clinical question in this patient.

Urinary 24-hour 5-HIAA
Urinary 24-hour 5-HIAA is the primary investigation for carcinoid syndrome, which is an important differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with flushing and diarrhoea. However, the presence of urticaria pigmentosa with a positive Darier's sign makes mastocytosis a much more likely diagnosis. While carcinoid syndrome should be considered, investigating for mastocytosis first is the more logical and targeted approach given the specific skin findings.

Urinary histamine metabolites
Urinary histamine metabolites, such as N-methylhistamine, can be elevated in mastocytosis as histamine is a key mediator released from mast cells. This test can be useful and supportive of the diagnosis, particularly in monitoring disease activity or in patients with symptoms of mast cell activation but normal tryptase levels. However, serum tryptase is more specific for mast cell burden and is the established and recommended first-line screening test for systemic mastocytosis in UK and international guidelines.

stem: A 41-year-old man develops itchy, polygonal, violaceous papules on the flexor aspect of his forearms. Some of these papules have coalesced to form plaques. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen planus
Lichen planus: purple, pruritic, papular, polygonal rash on flexor surfaces. Wickham's striae over surface. Oral involvement common. This condition is characterised by pruritic, polygonal, violaceous papules and plaques which often affect the flexor surfaces of the forearms. The description provided in the question fits this clinical picture perfectly. Lichen planus can also affect other parts of the body such as oral mucosa, genitals, scalp and nails.

Scabies
Scabies, on the other hand, typically present with intense pruritus that is worse at night. The lesions are usually small vesicles or papules, especially between fingers and toes, around the waist and in genital areas. While scabies can cause a rash on various parts of the body, it does not typically present with polygonal and violaceous papules.

Lichen sclerosus
Lichen sclerosus predominantly affects postmenopausal women although it can occur in men and children too. It primarily involves anogenital region but extragenital lesions can occur. The typical presentation is with white shiny patches on the skin that may become thin and wrinkled. Itching is common but not always present.

Morphea
Morphea, also known as localized scleroderma, causes patches of hard, discoloured skin that may be oval-shaped or linear. These patches initially appear reddish or purplish before becoming whitish or yellowish in the centre due to sclerosis (hardening). Morphea does not typically present as itchy violaceous papules.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder that commonly presents with well-defined erythematous plaques covered by silvery scales which are most often located on extensor surfaces like elbows and knees rather than flexural aspects. Psoriasis also has a variety of presentations such as guttate psoriasis or pustular psoriasis which do not match this case scenario.

stem: A 39-year-old female presents with well-demarcated red, scaly patches affecting the back of her elbows. These are making it hard to care for her newborn. She has been taking paracetamol regularly since her cesarean section 1 month ago and is not breastfeeding. At a medical review two weeks ago, she had been started on propranolol as required for anxiety, promethazine as required for insomnia, and a course of prednisolone for Bell's palsy. Which of the following is most likely to have precipitated her symptoms?
explanation:
Propranolol
Propranolol is a beta-blocker and these are known to exacerbate plaque psoriasis. The inflammatory effects occur primarily with fat-soluble beta-blockers, such as propranolol, as opposed to water-soluble ones, such as atenolol. This patient is presenting with typical features of plaque psoriasis, i.e. well-demarcated, scaly, erythematous patches affecting the extensor surfaces - in this case, the back of her elbows.

Promethazine
Promethazine is an antihistamine used for allergies, nausea and insomnia. It is not known to exacerbate psoriasis.

Paracetamol
Paracetamol, unlike aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, is not known to exacerbate psoriasis.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is often used as part of the treatment for psoriasis and would be very unlikely to exacerbate it.

Pregnancy-related progesterone rise
Psoriasis often improves during pregnancy. This is thought to be due to the rise in progesterone dampening the overactive immune response that triggers psoriasis. Indeed, psoriasis may flare up after delivery due to a fall in progesterone. Therefore, stating that a progesterone rise has caused the flare would be incorrect.

stem: A 4-year-old child, born in a refugee camp, is brought to the health clinic with clear evidence of malnutrition. The child has a characteristic rash with red crusted lesions in acral, periorificial and perianal distribution. Other clinical features include poor growth and cognitive development. What deficiency is most associated with this child's presentation?
explanation:
Zinc
Dermatitis in acral, peri-orificial and perianal distribution → zinc deficiency. This child has presented with acrodermatitis, a rash with red, crusted lesions affecting the acral distribution (the distal portion of the limbs i.e. hands, foot, and head i.e. ears, nose), periorificial and perianal distributions. Acquired acrodermatitis is a result of zinc deficiency due to reduced intake, increased zinc demands, malabsorption or rarely secondary to metabolic disorders. Primary acrodermatitis (also referred to as primary acrodermatitis enteropathica) is an inherited condition resulting in reduced intestinal zinc absorption secondary to a zinc transport defect. Other features of zinc deficiency include alopecia, night blindness, cognitive impairment and growth issues.

Iodine
Iodine deficiency mainly results in thyroid issues with iodine being needed to produce thyroxine. Iodine deficiency, therefore, results in hypothyroidism and a characteristic swelling of the thyroid gland known as a goitre. Iodine deficiency can also result in hair loss and skin changes in the form of myxoedema, which is a waxy, discoloured induration of the skin, generally affecting the pretibial areas.

Magnesium
Magnesium deficiency can result in multiple signs including tremors, muscle cramping, and muscle spasming. It can also result in nervous system dysfunctions, cardiac dysrhythmias and personality changes. In general skin changes and specific rashes are not associated with magnesium deficiency.

Niacin (vitamin B3)
Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency results in pellagra, a condition that classically results in the fours D's, diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia and eventually death. Skin changes in pellagra are common but are generally seen as a darkening and stiffening of the skin which may peel or bleed. A specific broad collar rash known as Casal collar is also associated with the condition, resulting in an erythematous, pigmented rash in the broad collar distribution (dermatomes C3 and C4).

Vitamin A
Vitamin A deficiency generally affects the eyes and is the commonest cause of blindness in low-income countries. Vitamin A is an important component of rhodopsin found in the retina and deficiency results in nyctalopia (night blindness), xerophthalmia (drying of the eyes), keratomalacia and eventually complete blindness. Skin changes are not commonly associated with vitamin A deficiency.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents with a swollen, itchy right eyelid. This has been ongoing for 10 days but the patient reports it has happened at least 5 times previously. Each time it self-resolved. On examination, there is erythema of the anterior lid margin and the base of the lashes of the right eye. Visual acuity, fundoscopy and cranial nerve examination are normal. You perform a systematic enquiry to elicit an underlying cause of this recurrent condition. What is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Otitis externa and blepharitis are common complications of seborrhoeic dermatitis. This is a history and examination suggesting anterior blepharitis. The most common underlying cause is seborrhoeic dermatitis. Seborrhoeic dermatitis normally causes eczematous lesions in the scalp, periorbital, auricular and nasolabial folds. It also can lead to otitis externa.

Atopic dermatitis
Atopic dermatitis (otherwise called atopic eczema) is the most common inflammatory skin condition. It can affect the face more commonly in childhood but does not commonly lead to blepharitis. Important complications of atopic dermatitis include staphylococcal infection and eczema herpeticum.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis does not typically cause blepharitis or any eye pathology. Complications of psoriasis include arthropathy as well as increased incidence of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease and venous thromboembolism.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis does not commonly cause blepharitis. However, ocular manifestations are common and include keratoconjunctivitis sicca, episcleritis, scleritis, corneal ulceration and keratitis. The examination findings in this question are not suggestive of any of these.

Rosacea
Rosacea is a condition causing flushing, telangiectasia, erythema and pustules of the face. It is a recognised cause of blepharitis but would be less common than seborrhoeic dermatitis in a 24-year-old male.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with unsightly toenails affecting the lateral three nails of the left foot. On examination the nails and brown and break easily. Nail scrapings demonstrate Trichophyton rubrum infection. What is the treatment of choice?
explanation:
Oral terbinafine for 12 weeks
Oral terbinafine for 12 weeks is the correct answer. This is because oral terbinafine is the first-line treatment for onychomycosis (fungal nail infection) caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum. A 12-week course of oral terbinafine is recommended for toenail infections, as they take longer to treat than fingernail infections due to slower nail growth.

Oral itraconazole for 4 weeks
Oral itraconazole for 4 weeks is incorrect because, although itraconazole can be used as an alternative treatment for onychomycosis, a 4-week course would not be sufficient to treat a toenail infection. Itraconazole is typically given in a pulsed dosing regimen, where the patient takes the medication daily for one week per month. For toenail infections, this regimen should be continued for at least three months.

Topical itraconazole for 2 weeks
Topical itraconazole for 2 weeks is not an appropriate choice because topical antifungal agents are generally less effective than oral medications in treating onychomycosis. Additionally, there are no UK guidelines recommending the use of topical itraconazole specifically for this condition.

Topical amorolfine for 6 weeks
Topical amorolfine for 6 weeks is also incorrect because topical treatments are typically reserved for mild cases of onychomycosis or when oral medications cannot be used due to contraindications or side effects. In this case, the patient has multiple affected nails and a confirmed T. rubrum infection, making oral therapy more suitable. Furthermore, if amorolfine were chosen as a topical treatment option, a longer duration of therapy (up to six months) would be required.

Oral itraconazole for 1 week
Oral itraconazole for 1 week is not a suitable treatment option because, as discussed earlier, itraconazole should be given in a pulsed dosing regimen for at least three months to effectively treat toenail onychomycosis. A 1-week course would not provide adequate treatment duration to eradicate the fungal infection.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with severe mucosal ulceration associated with the development of blistering lesions over her torso and arms. On examination the blisters are flaccid and easily ruptured when touched. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pemphigus vulgaris
The most likely diagnosis, in this case, is Pemphigus vulgaris. This condition is characterized by the presence of flaccid blisters and mucosal ulceration, which are easily ruptured when touched. Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disorder caused by autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3, which are proteins responsible for maintaining the integrity of keratinocyte adhesion in the epidermis. The loss of adhesion leads to intraepidermal blister formation.

Pemphigoid
Pemphigoid is another autoimmune blistering disorder, but it differs from pemphigus vulgaris in that it involves the formation of tense blisters rather than flaccid ones. In pemphigoid, autoantibodies target components of the basement membrane zone, leading to subepidermal blister formation. Due to the deeper location of these blisters compared to those seen in pemphigus vulgaris, they are more resistant to rupture.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic autoimmune skin condition associated with gluten sensitivity and coeliac disease. It presents as intensely pruritic papules, vesicles, and excoriations typically distributed symmetrically on extensor surfaces such as elbows, knees, and buttocks. Although it can present with blisters, these tend to be small and clustered rather than large and flaccid like those seen in pemphigus vulgaris.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales. It does not typically present with blistering or mucosal involvement as seen in this patient's presentation.

Epidermolysis bullosa
Epidermolysis bullosa refers to a group of rare inherited disorders characterized by fragility of the skin and mucous membranes leading to blister formation. These blisters can be induced by minor trauma or friction, but the onset of symptoms is usually in infancy or early childhood, making it an unlikely diagnosis for a 64-year-old woman presenting with new-onset blistering lesions.

stem: A 45-year-old male with known HIV attends the genitourinary medicine clinic for a review. A repeat CD4 count is taken: CD4 count 197 cells/mm³ (500-1,400 cells/mm³) The patient is started on co-trimoxazole, for prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, and continued on triple antiretroviral therapy of tenofovir, emtricitabine and raltegravir. Eight days later the patient presents to the emergency department. He reports starting to feel generally unwell 3 days prior to his attendance with intermittent fevers and generalised myalgia. The patient also reports that he has developed a rash and sore eyes and lips in the last 24 hours. On examination, the patient is found to have a tender area of erythema over the upper half of the torso with flaccid blistering of the skin. There is conjunctivitis in both eyes and tender blistering lesions are seen over the orobuccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Mucosal involvement is prominent and severe in Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Patients with HIV can present with multiple different dermatological conditions. Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is 100 times more common in patients with HIV. In this scenario, the patient was started on cotrimoxazole, a sulphonamide antibiotic, which is known to precipitate SJS. Presentations of SJS typically start within 1 week but can present up to one month after starting antibiotics. Where anticonvulsants are the causative agent, the presentation can be delayed by up to two months. SJS presents initially with a prodromal illness of intermittent fevers, myalgia and a sore throat. After a few days, a painful, erythematous skin rash develops abruptly over the trunk and arms. Blisters then appear and merge to form sheets of detached skin. Mucosal involvement is prominent and severe with at least two mucosal surfaces becoming involved. In this case, the patient developed conjunctivitis and painful ulcerations on the lips.

Bullous pemphigoid
Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense skin blistering and the mucosal surfaces are rarely involved. There is no increased association with HIV also.

Kaposi sarcoma
Kaposi sarcoma is a condition more commonly seen in immunocompromised patients. It can present anywhere on the skin or mucosal surfaces, presenting initially as a painless erythematous lesion and can progress into painful ulcerations. The lesions are initially more discrete and present much more slowly than is reported here.

Pruritic papular eruption of HIV
Pruritic papular eruption of HIV is a diagnosis of exclusion in patients with HIV presenting with a rash. Here there are other more likely differential diagnoses such as SJS. The condition can present at any time during HIV infection and presents with small erythematous papules which are intensely itchy. The mucosal surfaces are also spared.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome has been reported in the literature to occur in adult patients with HIV, however, this is extremely rare. It has a greater association in adults with chronic renal failure, but again this is still rare. This condition is typically seen in children under 5 years of age. The presentation is similar to SJS with a blistering, painful, erythematous skin rash extending over the body surfaces. Importantly, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome does not involve the mucosal surfaces, whereas SJS does.

stem: A 33-year-old lady presents complaining of facial discolouration. She is 26 weeks pregnant. So far it has been an uncomplicated pregnancy. She has a background of rheumatoid arthritis but has been off treatment for 2 years. On examination she has a large, flat, symmetrical, brown-pigmented patch across her cheeks, forehead, nose and upper lip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Melasma
The correct answer is Melasma, also known as chloasma or 'mask of pregnancy'. This condition presents as symmetrical hyperpigmented patches typically affecting the face, particularly the cheeks, forehead, upper lip, and nose - precisely matching this patient's presentation. It commonly occurs during pregnancy due to increased levels of oestrogen and progesterone stimulating melanocytes. The timing during pregnancy (26 weeks) is typical, and the description of a flat, brown patch is characteristic.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) can present with a malar rash ('butterfly rash'), but this typically appears as an erythematous, raised rash rather than brown pigmentation. While SLE can occur during pregnancy and the patient has an autoimmune background (rheumatoid arthritis), the description of the skin changes is not consistent with the malar rash of SLE.

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP) typically presents in the third trimester or immediately postpartum with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques, usually starting in the striae of the abdomen. It does not cause facial hyperpigmentation and would not present with the described symmetrical brown patches.

Rosacea
Rosacea presents with erythema, telangiectasia, papules, and pustules primarily affecting the central face. It appears red rather than brown and often has a more inflammatory appearance. Patients typically experience flushing and may have ocular symptoms. The description of brown pigmentation does not fit with rosacea.

Vitiligo
Vitiligo causes depigmented patches due to destruction of melanocytes, resulting in white patches rather than hyperpigmentation. It can affect any area of the body and would not present as brown patches. While it can be symmetrical, the complete absence of pigment rather than increased pigmentation makes this diagnosis incorrect.

stem: A 52-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman presents to the dermatology department. She has noticed a patch of pigmented skin on her toe, which has been slowly enlarging over the past five months. On examination, she has pigmentation of the nail bed of her great toe, affecting the adjacent cuticle and proximal nail fold. Which subtype of melanoma would you expect to present in this manner?
explanation:
Acral lentiginous melanoma
Acral lentiginous melanoma: Pigmentation of nail bed affecting proximal nail fold suggests melanoma (Hutchinson's sign) Acral lentiginous melanoma is the rarest form of melanoma overall, but the commonest form of melanoma in people with darker skin. Hence it is important to be able to recognise. Acral lentiginous melanoma mostly affects people over the age of 40 and is equally common in males and females. It is not related to sun exposure. It typically presents as an enlarging discoloured skin patch on the palms, fingers, soles or toes with the characteristics of other flat forms of melanoma. It can arise in the nail unit, appearing as general discolouration or irregular pigmented bands running longitudinally along the nail plate and is called subungual melanoma when it arises in the matrix. This patient has subungual acral lentiginous melanoma with an important clinical clue of this called 'Hutchinson's nail sign'. This sign is characterised by extension of the nail bed, matrix and nail plate pigmentation to the adjacent cuticle and proximal or lateral nail folds.

Superficial spreading melanoma
Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common type of melanoma and typically presents as an irregularly shaped, pigmented lesion on sun-exposed areas of the skin. It is less likely to present in the nail unit.

Lentigo maligna melanoma
Lentigo maligna melanoma typically presents as a slowly enlarging, irregularly pigmented macule on sun-damaged skin, usually in older individuals. It is less likely to present in the nail unit.

Nodular melanoma
Nodular melanoma is a more aggressive form of melanoma that typically presents as a rapidly growing, darkly pigmented nodule. It is less likely to present as a slowly enlarging, pigmented patch in the nail unit.

Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is a rare form of melanoma that lacks the typical pigmentation and can appear as a non-pigmented or flesh-colored lesion. It is less likely to present as a pigmented lesion in the nail unit.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to his GP with an itchy rash affecting his back, axillae and face. He has never had this before. It has been present for 2 weeks and it has become more itchy recently over the last week. He is otherwise well. On examination, there is greasy erythema of both axillae, upper back and nasolabial folds with evidence of mild excoriation. All areas of erythema are scaly and cool to the touch. Skin swabs of the face grow Staphylococcus aureus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Seborrhoeic dermatitis
An itchy rash affecting the face and scalp distribution is commonly caused by seborrhoeic dermatitis. An itchy, scaly, greasy rash distributed across the face, scalp, upper back, chest and skin flexures is typical of seborrhoeic dermatitis. This is most common in middle-aged adults. Diagnosis is clinical. The presence of Staphylococcus aureus is non-specific and does not necessarily indicate infection. Whilst chronic infection can develop secondary to excoriation, there is little evidence in this patient of cellulitis. Features of infection would include pain, spreading erythema, warmth to touch, or systemic upset.

Cellulitis
Features of infection would include pain, spreading erythema, warmth to touch, or systemic upset. There is little evidence in this patient of cellulitis.

Discoid lupus erythematosus
The skin lesions in discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) are typically indurated plaques rather than diffuse erythema which is seen in this patient. The lesions can affect the face, neck, ears and scalp. Younger women are typically affected and DLE is more common in skin of colour.

Psoriasis
The skin lesions in psoriasis are typically larger and clearly defined. They are silvery white or shiny in the skin folds, are symmetrically distributed over the scalp, elbows and knees and are persistent without treatment. This patient's rash has been intermittent.

Rosacea
The first stages of rosacea are facial flushing followed by papules and pustules. There would not typically be involvement of the axillae or back. Rosacea would also be unlikely in a 30-year-old man.
