stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with several months of a non-healing ulcer on her left lower leg. It has steadily increased in size and intermittently discharges pus. She denies any pain. The patient explains that the ulcer overlies a scar from an old burn injury almost 30 years ago. On examination, a ulcer of approximately 2cm diameter is noted on the left lower leg. It is surrounded by scar tissue. The ulcer is flat and indurated, with elevated margins, and is pink and white. It bleeds upon contact during examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma
A non-healing painless ulcer associated with a chronic scar is indicative of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). This patient's lesion is suspicious of a Marjolin ulcer. This is the development of a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) at the site of an old scar. Typically, burn scars are involved, and the SCC develops some 20 to 30 years after the original injury. The mechanism of this is not completely understood. Marjolin ulcers typically present as nonhealing sores and often bleed and discharge pus. This presentation warrants urgent referral for further investigation.

Arterial ulcer
An arterial ulcer would instead have a deeper, 'punched-out' appearance. The patient would likely describe pain on elevation of the leg and on walking. The description here is instead more suggestive of SCC.

Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is not as frequently associated with scar tissue as SCC. It would appear differently to the lesion described above - typically a well-defined nodule with pearly, rolled edges.

Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma is less commonly associated with scar tissue, although would also warrant urgent referral. It would appear differently, with dark pigmentation being a defining feature.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum typically starts as a blister or papule at a site of minor injury and rapidly becomes painful, dusky-purple and purulent. This does not fit with the lesion here, which is more suggestive of SCC.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a recurring itchy rash on his hands and feet. He frequently travels to the middle east on business. He has had unprotected sex recently on one of these trips. On examination, there is an itchy vesicular rash on the palms and soles with areas of excoriation and erythema. Exposure to what factor is the likely precipitant of this particular rash?
explanation:
Humidity
Pompholyx eczema may be precipitated by humidity (e.g. sweating) and high temperatures. The description of the rash (recurrent vesicles affecting the palms and soles associated with erythema) is typical of pompholyx eczema. This can be precipitated by humidity. His frequent travel to the middle east, which is an especially humid region, may be contributory.

Chlamydia
Chlamydia is incorrect. Keratoderma blennorrhagica may be precipitated by chlamydia in the context of reactive arthritis. This rash is found on the soles of the feet but can also affect the palms. It can be vesico-pustular but tends to have a waxy brown appearance rather than being erythematous and itchy.

Cold
Cold is incorrect. This may precipitate Raynaud's phenomenon but not pompholyx eczema.

Sunlight
Sunlight is incorrect. This can precipitate many conditions such as lupus and polymorphic light eruption. However, it is humidity rather than sunlight that precipitates pompholyx.

Syphilis
Syphilis is incorrect. This can cause a rash on the palms and soles but it is typically macular.

stem: A 59-year-old patient presents to dermatology outpatients clinic with a three-month history of discolouration of the skin on his back. On examination, there are patchy areas of mild hypopigmentation covering large areas of the back. You suspect a diagnosis of pityriasis versicolor. What is the likely causative organism?
explanation:
Malassezia
Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. Pityriasis versicolour is caused by infection with Malassezia fungus. Initial treatment is with topical anti-fungals such as ketoconazole shampoo.

Epidermophyton
Epidermophyton, Trichophyton and Micosporum are dermatophytes and cause fungal nail infections and ringworm.

Histoplasma capsulatum
Histoplasma is a fungi that can cause pneumonia in immuno-compromised patients.

Micosporum
Epidermophyton, Trichophyton and Micosporum are dermatophytes and cause fungal nail infections and ringworm.

Trichophyton
Epidermophyton, Trichophyton and Micosporum are dermatophytes and cause fungal nail infections and ringworm.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with a lesion on his right lower leg. He states that it has been growing in size over the last 3 months. On examination, you note a 2x3cm ulcerated crusted lump over the right anterior shin. A CT scan is performed: CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis No evidence of regional lymph node involvement or distant metastases What treatment is indicated given the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Surgical excision
Surgical excision is correct. Surgical excision is the preferred treatment for localised disease. Surgical excision with 4mm margins is preferred if the lesion is <20mm in diameter, and with 6mm margins if the lesion is >20mm in diameter.

Chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy
Chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy is incorrect. Although initial surgical excision cures 95% of patients, a minority of cutaneous SCCs are considered unresectable, either locally advanced or with unresectable regional lymph nodes or distant metastases. These patients are offered systemic treatments with chemo-immunotherapy. Two checkpoint inhibitors, cemiplimab and pembrolizumab, have demonstrated a high response rate and survival with fewer toxicities than other available systemic agents. The CT scan in this case did not demonstrate any regional lymph node involvement or distant metastases and thus systemic treatment can be avoided if the lesion can be fully resected.

Cryotherapy
Cryotherapy is incorrect. Cryotherapy is used for some early squamous cell cancers, especially in people who can not have surgery. Superficial, in situ, or SCC less and equal to 1 cm has been successfully treated with cryosurgery with results comparable to traditional surgical excision. In this case, the lesion is > 1cm and therefore surgery is required.

Diclofenac topical gel
Diclofenac topical gel is incorrect. This can be used to treat actinic keratosis (the most common precursor lesion for squamous cell carcinoma). Actinic keratosis may be solitary but there are often multiple keratoses. The appearance varies. However, classically they present with flat to slightly raised, scaly, and crusty lesions which sometimes have a raised horn shape or bump. They usually occur on sun exposure sites (e.g. the scalp). In this case, the presence of ulceration favours a diagnosis of SCC.

Mohs micrographic surgery
Mohs micrographic surgery is incorrect. Mohs micrographic surgery may be used in high-risk patients and in cosmetically important sites (e.g. face). Mohs surgery is designed to minimise scarring at the outset, by creating the smallest post-surgical wound possible.

stem: A patient who is suspected of having dermatitis herpetiformis undergoes a skin biopsy. Which one of the following antibodies is most likely to be found in the dermis?
explanation:
IgA
Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic blistering skin condition that is characterised by the presence of IgA deposits in the dermis. It is associated with gluten sensitivity and coeliac disease. The IgA antibodies are directed against tissue transglutaminase (tTG) and epidermal transglutaminase (eTG), which are found in the dermis.

IgM
IgM is not typically associated with dermatitis herpetiformis. This type of immunoglobulin is often the first antibody produced in response to an initial exposure to an antigen. It's usually involved in the primary immune response, but it's not specific to any particular skin conditions.

IgD
IgD also isn't typically related to dermatitis herpetiformis. IgD functions mainly as an antigen receptor on B cells that have not been exposed to antigens. It has been shown to control B cell activation and suppression, but its function isn't well understood.

IgE
IgE antibodies are associated with allergic reactions and parasitic infections, rather than dermatitis herpetiformis. They bind to allergens and trigger histamine release from mast cells and basophils, leading to inflammation. Conditions such as atopic dermatitis or urticaria would be more likely associated with elevated levels of IgE.

IgG
IgG antibodies are not typically found in high concentrations in the dermis of patients with dermatitis herpetiformis either. IgG antibodies are the most common type of antibody found in blood circulation, they provide long-term protection after infection or vaccination and play a role in many autoimmune diseases but aren't specifically linked to this condition.

stem: Which one of the following side-effects is least recognised in patients taking isotretinoin?
explanation:
Hypertension
Hypertension is not listed in the British National Formulary as a side-effect.

Teratogenicity
Isotretinoin adverse effects include teratogenicity - females MUST be taking contraception.

Nose bleeds
Isotretinoin adverse effects include nose bleeds.

Depression
Isotretinoin adverse effects include low mood (depression).

Raised triglycerides
Isotretinoin adverse effects include raised triglycerides.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to his doctor with a 2-week history of rash. The rash has spread and on examination, there are multiple erythematous, slightly raised oval lesions with a fine-scale confined to the outer aspects of the lesions. The distribution of the lesions is like a fir tree across his trunk and back. He does not feel unwell. A diagnosis of pityriasis rosea is suspected. Which organism has been implicated in the aetiology of this condition?
explanation:
Herpes hominis virus 7 (HHV-7)
Herpes hominis virus 7 (HHV-7) is thought to play a role in the aetiology of pityriasis rosea. The answer is herpes hominis virus 7 (HHV-7).

Parvovirus B-19
Parvovirus B-19 is associated with slapped cheek syndrome.

Streptococcus agalactiae
Streptococcus agalactiae is a Lancefield Group B streptococcus associated with neonatal meningitis.

Coxsackie B virus
Coxsackie B virus is an enterovirus associated with Bornholm disease, pericarditis, myocarditis and aseptic meningitis.

Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus pyogenes is a Lancefield Group A streptococcus implicated in the pathogenesis of scarlet fever.

stem: Which one of the following features is least likely to be seen in a patient with pellagra?
explanation:
Dysphagia
Dysphagia is the least likely feature to be seen in a patient with pellagra.

Diarrhoea
Diarrhoea is a common feature of pellagra, often referred to as one of the three Ds (diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia).

Depression
Depression is quite a common early finding in patients with pellagra.

Dermatitis
Dermatitis is a hallmark feature of pellagra, often presenting as a symmetric, sunburn-like rash on sun-exposed areas.

Dementia
Dementia is a common feature of pellagra, often referred to as one of the three Ds (diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia).

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to his GP extremely concerned that he has scabies. His boyfriend has informed him he has recently been treated and his GP is able to identify the characteristic burrows in his finger webs. He has no other skin conditions, or drug/food allergies. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate first line?
options: Oral prednisolone for 1 week, with antihistamine cream applied PRN for itch
Malathion 0.5% lotion applied to all skin, rinsed after 12 hours, with re-treatment after 1 week
Daily salt water baths + wash all bedding and clothing at minimum 80 degrees
Permethrin 5% cream applied to all skin, rinsed after 12 hours with re-treatment after 1 week
Topical mupirocin cream applied to all skin, with re-treatment after 1 week
explanation:
Permethrin 5% cream applied to all skin, rinsed after 12 hours with re-treatment after 1 week
Permethrin cream, applied to all skin then rinsed after 12 hours is the current 1st line treatment for scabies.

Oral prednisolone for 1 week, with antihistamine cream applied PRN for itch
Steroids are sometimes used by dermatologists in treatment of resistant scabies/scabies pruritus but this is under specialist guidance only.

Malathion 0.5% lotion applied to all skin, rinsed after 12 hours, with re-treatment after 1 week
Malathion is used 2nd line and is rinsed after 24 hours.

Daily salt water baths + wash all bedding and clothing at minimum 80 degrees
Salt water bathing is not a recommended treatment.

Topical mupirocin cream applied to all skin, with re-treatment after 1 week
Mupirocin cream is used to eradicate MRSA in asymptomatic hospital inpatients.

stem: A 21-year-old female presents to the dermatology department with an intensely pruritic erythematous rash on the palmar aspect of her hands and the arch of her left foot. She complains of a burning sensation. Her past medical history includes gastro-oesophageal reflux disease for which she takes omeprazole but takes no other medication. Family history includes asthma and type 2 diabetes. She recently returned from a 4 week trip to Thailand. On examination, there are crops of deep blisters on both the dorsal and volar aspect of her hands and the sole of her foot. There are also areas of dry erythematous fissures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pompholyx dermatitis
Pompholyx eczema is a subtype of eczema characterised by an intensely pruritic rash on the palms and soles. This patient is presenting with characteristic signs of pompholyx dermatitis (vesicular or dyshidrotic dermatitis). Her recent stay in a hot humid climate (Thailand) may have precipitated this flare-up. This type of dermatitis is particularly resistant to treatment. Topical treatments are typically ineffective because of the thick horny layer of skin on the hands and feet.

Herpes virus infection
Herpes virus infection can cause a vesicular rash but it is most typically around the mouth (HSV1) or in the genitals (HSV2). Eczema herpeticum can occur in patients with existing atopic dermatitis; it is typically a widespread vesicular rash with associated constitutional symptoms.

Irritant contact dermatitis
Irritant contact dermatitis represents an injury response to an irritant. Anyone can suffer from this, however, an irritant threshold may be different depending on the characteristics of your skin e.g. bleach can affect someone with sensitive skin in very small amounts but may need a significant amount of splash to affect another person. The history is not suggestive of this pathology.

Allergic contact dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction resulting in a rash that appears 48 to 72 hours after exposure to an irritant. The history is not suggestive of this pathology.

Fixed drug eruption
Fixed drug eruption is an important differential but presents as well-demarcated erythematous oval lesions with or without a blister.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the haematology clinic with a 6-month history of episodic flushing and abdominal pain. Examination reveals multiple brown macules on her trunk that develop wheals when rubbed. Blood film shows monocytosis. Serum tryptase 28 ng/mL (<11.4) What is the most appropriate next investigation to establish a definitive diagnosis?
explanation:
Bone marrow biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy is the gold-standard investigation used to diagnose systemic mastocytosis. This patient presents with classic features including urticaria pigmentosa (brown macules that wheal when rubbed - Darier's sign), flushing, abdominal pain, monocytosis, and significantly elevated serum tryptase levels. While elevated tryptase (>20 ng/mL persistently) is a minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis, definitive diagnosis requires bone marrow examination. The biopsy allows for histological assessment of mast cell infiltration, immunohistochemistry to identify aberrant mast cell markers (such as CD25 and CD2), and molecular testing for the KIT D816V mutation, which is present in over 90% of cases. These findings form the major diagnostic criteria according to WHO classification.

24-hour urinary histamine
24-hour urinary histamine can be elevated in systemic mastocytosis and may support the diagnosis, but it is primarily used to monitor disease activity rather than establish the initial diagnosis. It is not specific for mastocytosis and can be elevated in other conditions causing mast cell degranulation.

Chromogranin A level
Chromogranin A level is a neuroendocrine marker that would be more relevant in investigating carcinoid syndrome, which can present with flushing but would not typically cause the skin lesions or monocytosis seen in this case.

CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis might identify organomegaly or lymphadenopathy associated with systemic mastocytosis, but imaging alone cannot provide the definitive diagnosis required for this condition.

Flow cytometry of peripheral blood
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood is not routinely used in diagnosing systemic mastocytosis as circulating mast cells are typically very low in number, even in systemic disease. The abnormal mast cells are predominantly found in tissue, particularly bone marrow.

stem: A 62-year-old male is referred to dermatology with a lesion over his shin. On examination shiny, painless areas of yellow skin over the shin are found with abundant telangiectasia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum
Diabetes, waxy yellow shin lesions - necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. The correct answer is Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. This condition is a rare skin disorder of unclear aetiology, often associated with diabetes mellitus. It typically presents as shiny, atrophic, yellowbrown plaques on the shins with telangiectasia and occasional ulceration. The patient's age, the location of the lesion and its description fit this diagnosis.

Pretibial myxoedema
Pretibial myxoedema is incorrect because it is a cutaneous manifestation of Graves' disease (an autoimmune thyroid condition), rather than a primary skin condition. It presents as non-pitting oedema on the lower legs (shin area). The skin changes can range from subtle thickening to nodular or plaque-like accumulations of mucin in the dermis, which may be mistaken for cellulitis or lymphoedema.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum also does not fit this clinical picture. Erythema nodosum presents as painful, erythematous nodules most commonly located over the anterior shin areas. Unlike necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum, these lesions are painful and not characterised by yellowish discolouration or telangiectasia.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is another incorrect choice. Pyoderma gangrenosum usually starts as a small pustule that progresses to a large ulcer with violaceous borders. Although it can occur anywhere on the body, it most commonly affects the legs. Pyoderma gangrenosum would not present as shiny yellow patches with telangiectasias.

Syphilis
Finally, Syphilis, specifically secondary syphilis could potentially cause skin manifestations but these would typically be widespread symmetrical rash which involves palm and soles along with systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Primary syphilis would present with a painless chancre, typically genitally located. Neither stages fit this case presentation.

stem: You review a 50-year-old man who has a history of ischaemic heart disease and psoriasis. Over the past two weeks he has experienced a significant worsening of the plaque psoriasis affecting his elbows and knees. His medications have recently been altered at the cardiology clinic. Which one of the following medications is most likely to have exacerbated his psoriasis?
explanation:
Atenolol
Beta-blockers are known to exacerbate plaque psoriasis. The correct answer is atenolol. Beta-blockers like atenolol are well-known to potentially exacerbate psoriasis. The mechanism is thought to be related to decreased cyclic AMP levels in skin cells, which affects cell proliferation and differentiation. This is a class effect of beta-blockers and can occur with both selective (like atenolol) and non-selective agents.

Nicorandil
Nicorandil is a potassium channel opener used in angina. While it can cause oral ulceration as a side effect, it is not typically associated with worsening psoriasis.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor used for hypercholesterolaemia. Some studies have actually suggested statins may have beneficial effects in psoriasis due to their anti-inflammatory properties.

Verapamil
Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker used in angina and hypertension. Unlike beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers are not known to exacerbate psoriasis and may sometimes be used as alternative agents in patients where beta-blockers are contraindicated.

Isosorbide mononitrate
Isosorbide mononitrate is a nitrate used for angina prophylaxis. It works through vasodilation and has no known association with psoriasis exacerbation. Common side effects include headache and hypotension but not skin problems.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to her GP for lesions on her arms which appeared suddenly several days ago. Her mother persuaded her to attend the appointment - the patient herself was not keen. When asked about the lesions, she does not give a clear history of their appearance/progression. Her past medical history includes mild asthma, depression and generalised anxiety disorder. On examination, she has linear, well-demarcated skin lesions on both arms. They do not appear dry or scaly. They appear excoriated. There are no obvious signs of infection. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
explanation:
Dermatitis artefacta
Linear, well-demarcated skin lesions that appear suddenly, with 'la belle indifference' → ?dermatitis artefacta The description here points strongly towards dermatitis artefacta, also known as factitious dermatitis. This is a rare psycho-dermatological condition involving self-inflicted skin lesions. Patients demonstrate apathy/indifference toward the lesions, denying their own involvement, and are prompted to engage with healthcare professionals by relatives or friends. Regarding management, good rapport is crucial. Direct confrontation is often detrimental, and patients should be co-managed by psychiatrists and dermatologists.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterised by itchy blisters across the body. It is linked to coeliac disease, of which there is no mention in the stem.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus appears as flat-topped, itchy raised violaceous papules, often in clusters. It is thought to be an autoimmune condition. This is not consistent with the scenario above.

Neurotic excoriations
Neurotic excoriations are also psychocutaneous manifestations. These similarly result in skin lesions from picking and excoriating, but patients actively admit their own involvement in creating the lesions. This is unlike dermatitis artefacta, where patients deny involvement.

Trichotillomania
Trichotillomania is the action of repeated hair-pulling, resulting in hair loss. Patients usually experience relief once they have performed this action. Although this is another psychocutaneous condition, the scenario here refers to dermatitis artefacta.

stem: A 24-year-old Greek woman attends an endocrinology clinic with facial hair that she finds embarrassing and upsetting. Bloods tests show the following: Testosterone 1.7 nmol/L (0.2 - 1.7) TSH 3.8mU/L (0.27 - 4.2) Free T4 18pmol/L (12 - 22) Prolactin 325 (<700) Cortisol 422 nmol/L (140 - 690) Ultrasound abdomen: 7 immature follicles within the left ovary, 2 immature follicles within the right ovary, both ovaries normal volume. Normal appearance of other pelvic viscera. Her periods are normal, her BMI is 20kg/m2, and she has one child aged 2. She is keen to reduce the appearance of her facial hair. What treatment would you recommend?
explanation:
Topical eflornithine
Topical eflornithine is the treatment of choice for facial hirsutism. In around 20% of women with hirsutism, no cause is identified. Hirsutism is more common in those of Mediterranean or Middle Eastern descent. Causes of hirsutism can include drugs (e.g. steroids, ciclosporin, danazol), polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), and androgen-secreting tumours. PCOS is defined by the Rotterdam criteria and can be diagnosed if a patient meets two of the following: Oligo or an-ovulation, biochemical and or clinical signs of hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries (i.e. More than or equal to 12 follicles in each ovary or raised ovarian volume). The patient in the stem does not meet the Rotterdam criteria. Following the screening tests done, no specific cause has been found for her hirsutism. Topical eflornithine acts on the hair follicle to inhibit hair growth. It is the first-line treatment for facial hirsutism and results are usually seen after 6-8 weeks. Hair growth returns if the use of this treatment is stopped.

Combined oral contraceptive pill
Combined oral contraceptive pill is a second-line treatment for premenopausal hirsutism.

Cyproterone acetate
Cyproterone acetate is an anti-androgen that is used to treat androgen-dependent conditions including excessive hair growth. It is not first-line in the treatment of facial hirsutism.

Electrolysis
Electrolysis is a method of hair reduction that destroys hair follicles. It is painful and impractical for larger areas. It could be an option, but topical eflornithine is recommended first-line.

Metformin
Metformin is used to improve hirsutism for PCOS patients. In this case, the patient does not have symptoms of PCOS - her periods are regular, testosterone levels are normal.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with itchy blisters on her hands. She says the lesions first appeared on her fingers and then spread to her palms. She complains of intense pruritus resistant to over the counter ointments. She is an art student and recently got a summer job at a children's summer camp where she leads athletics and arts and crafts sessions. On examination, there are tense vesicles on her fingers and the palms of her hands without erythema. Her past medical history is significant for asthma which is well-controlled with a salbutamol inhaler. She takes cetirizine daily during the summer months for hay fever. Which of the following is most likely to precipitate this condition?
explanation:
High temperatures in summer
Pompholyx eczema may be precipitated by humidity (e.g. sweating) and high temperatures. Pompholyx eczema (also known as dyshidrotic dermatitis) is a common condition characterised by an intensely pruritic vesicular eruption on the palms and soles. Although the aetiology is unknown, triggers include humidity (e.g., increased sweating due to climate, hyperhidrosis).

Exposure to PVA glue
Triggers for pompholyx eczema include irritants such as water, detergents, and metals (nickel), but not specifically PVA glue.

Cetirizine use
Cetirizine is used for hay fever and is not a known trigger for pompholyx eczema.

Beta-blocker use
Beta-blocker use is not a known trigger for pompholyx eczema.

stem: A 33-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a four-day history of a painful rash. He tells you it started around his mouth and he thought it was cold sores but later spread over his cheeks, neck and shoulders. He visited his GP 2 days ago due to a rash that developed on his hands, this remains stable. On examination, he has multiple coalescing, crusted vesicles on an erythematous oedematous base over his neck and shoulders. There are clusters of vesicles on his wrists. He has a history of mild eczema that he manages with emollients. Other medications include carbamazepine, haloperidol and codeine. Which of the following is the next best management?
explanation:
Intravenous aciclovir
Same-day referral to a dermatologist is recommended if eczema herpeticum is suspected. This patient has eczema herpeticum (caused by herpes simplex virus), this condition is associated with significant morbidity and mortality so warrants an urgent dermatology referral (<48 hours). Ophthalmology referral is warranted if eye involvement is suspected. Most cases require IV antivirals as systemic dissemination and viremia can occur especially in immunocompromised patients.

Oral flucloxacillin
Oral flucloxacillin would be helpful if a bacterial infection was suspected, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with eczema herpeticum, which is caused by a viral infection.

Stop all medication
In patients with an acute rash where toxic epidermal necrolysis is suspected, all medication should be stopped and the patient should be transferred to a burns unit. However, this rash is characterised by epidermal detachment affecting >30% of body surface area, mucous membrane involvement, and a positive Nikolsky sign, which are not present in this case.

Empiric ceftazidime and vancomycin
Empiric ceftazidime and vancomycin would be appropriate if a severe bacterial infection was suspected, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with eczema herpeticum, which is a viral infection.

Oral corticosteroids
Systemic corticosteroids may be helpful in severe allergic drug reactions, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with eczema herpeticum, which is a viral infection.

stem: A 31-year-old woman develops with painful, purple lesions on her shins. Which one of the following medications is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Combined oral contraceptive pill
The correct answer is Combined oral contraceptive pill. This woman's presentation is suggestive of erythema nodosum, a type of panniculitis characterised by painful, red or purple nodules that typically appear on the shins. The combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) can cause a wide range of side effects and has been associated with the development of erythema nodosum, though the exact mechanism remains unclear. It may be related to hormonal changes induced by the COCP.

Montelukast
Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist used in the management of asthma, is not typically associated with skin reactions such as erythema nodosum. Its common side effects include gastrointestinal disturbances and headache.

Lansoprazole
The proton pump inhibitor Lansoprazole is also unlikely to be responsible for this woman's symptoms. Side effects are usually gastrointestinal in nature, including diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal pain. Skin reactions are rare and when they do occur they tend to be rashes rather than specific lesions like erythema nodosum.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate, an antiepileptic drug, can cause a variety of side effects but these predominantly involve the gastrointestinal system (e.g., nausea), central nervous system (e.g., drowsiness), or haematological abnormalities (e.g., thrombocytopenia). While it can cause some skin reactions, these are usually more generalised rashes rather than erythema nodosum.

Carbimazole
Carbimazole, which is used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism, commonly causes side effects such as pruritus and rash but these are typically diffuse rather than localised to specific areas like the shins. More serious side effects include agranulocytosis and liver dysfunction but these are not relevant to this case.

stem: A 69-year-old woman was evaluated following the development of a rash on her lower limbs for the last two weeks, worsening breathlessness and weight loss. This eruption started as a small erythematous annular patch, slowly enlarging into polycyclic patches with a wood-grain appearance over the lateral aspects of her left thigh. The patient had a background of atrial fibrillation on warfarin and hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. She has 45 pack year history of smoking with underlying COPD managed with regular inhalers and home nebulisers. She complained of losing 10kg in weight over the last six months. Her symptoms were not being managed using her inhalers and nebulisers. Based on the history and clinical findings, what is the correct diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema gyratum repens
Erythema gyratum repens is a paraneoplastic eruption with a 'woodgrain' pattern and figurate erythema commonly seen in patients with lung cancer. Erythema gyratum repens - associated with internal malignancies - is characterised by a number of concentric, erythematous, from either flat to slightly raised bands with fine white scale in waves located at the leading edge of erythema. Their appearance may represent a wood-grain pattern. It can often precede a diagnosis of typically lung cancer by an average of nine months.

Erythema annulare centrifugum
Erythema annulare centrifugum is defined by the presence of expanding, erythematous annular lesions. Its cause is unknown but likely due to drugs, insect bites, food & infections.

Mycosis fungoides
Mycosis fungoides is a form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterised by itchy, erythematous scattered patches and plaques.

Erythema chronicum migrans
Erythema chronicum migrans is the classical rash caused by Lyme disease following a tick bite. It starts off as a red macule/papule developing into an expanding patch of erythema with a classic bull's eye appearance.

Tinea corporis
Tinea corporis is a superficial fungal ringworm infection.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is diagnosed with a number of erythematous, rough lesions on the back of her hands. A diagnosis of actinic keratoses is made. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Topical fluorouracil cream
The correct answer is Topical fluorouracil cream. Actinic keratoses (AKs) are rough, scaly patches on the skin that are caused by excessive exposure to the sun. They can potentially develop into squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer. Therefore, treatment is recommended to prevent this progression. In the UK, according to NICE guidelines, topical fluorouracil cream is considered first-line therapy for multiple AKs. This medication works by interfering with the DNA in skin cells, preventing their growth and causing them to die.

Reassurance
Reassurance is incorrect because although actinic keratoses are not malignant themselves, they have the potential to progress into squamous cell carcinoma. Hence it's important to treat them rather than simply reassuring the patient.

Urgent referral to a dermatologist
Urgent referral to a dermatologist isn't necessary unless there's suspicion of malignant transformation or if initial treatments fail - neither of which we're told is applicable in this case scenario.

Review in 3 months
Review in 3 months without any treatment intervention may allow for unnecessary progression of the lesions and hence is not an appropriate management strategy.

Topical betnovate
Topical betnovate, a corticosteroid cream, is also not a suitable treatment for actinic keratoses as it doesn't target the abnormal proliferation of keratinocytes seen in these lesions. Instead, it's primarily used for conditions involving inflammation and itching such as eczema and dermatitis.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a three-week history of an itchy rash over the face and upper chest. His only past medical history is HIV for which he is poorly compliant with his antiretroviral medications. On examination, areas of erythema over the eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and upper chest are noted. Excoriations surrounding the rash are present. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Topical ketoconazole
Seborrhoeic dermatitis - first-line treatment is topical ketoconazole. This man has presented with a rash consistent with seborrhoeic dermatitis, which he is at particular risk of given his past medical history of HIV. The first-line treatment for this condition is topical ketoconazole.

Oral fluconazole
Oral fluconazole can be used to treat various fungal infections and has a role in antifungal prophylaxis in HIV however is not used in the treatment of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone may be used in short courses to treat extensive inflammatory skin disease such as atopic dermatitis, however has no role in seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Topical hydrocortisone
Topical steroids such as hydrocortisone can be used for short periods to treat seborrhoeic dermatitis however are not the most appropriate initial therapy.

UV therapy
UV therapy has a role in various skin diseases, notably psoriasis, however is not used in the management of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of loss of libido and impotence. He also states that he has developed a rash around his anus. He has a background of alcohol excess and he currently drinks 60 units per week. On examination, you note red, crusted lesions around his anus. Blood results are as follows: Hb 146 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 172 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) MCV 86 fL (80 - 100) Testosterone 1.6 nmol/L (8.7 - 29) FSH 0.2 IU/L (0 - 6.0) LH 0.6 IU/mL (1.24 to 7.8) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Zinc deficiency
The combination of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and peri-anal dermatitis favour the diagnosis of zinc deficiency. Other features can include cognitive impairment, alopecia and hepatosplenomegaly. Alcohol excess as seen in this case is a well-known risk factor for zinc deficiency.

B12 deficiency
The normal FBC and MCV make B12 deficiency unlikely. This condition presents with a macrocytic anaemia. Mucocutaneous features include glossitis and angular cheilitis.

Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency would generally present with a microcytic anaemia. It is important to remember that microcytosis can predate the onset of anaemia. Mucocutaneous features include angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis, pruritus, dry skin, and koilonychia.

Niacin deficiency
Niacin deficiency causes pellagra which is characterised by the classic triad of diarrhoea, dermatitis, and dementia. Mucocutaneous features include a photosensitive rash and anogenital and mucosal lesions. Genital lesions can present with redness, erosions, and maceration.

Vitamin C deficiency
Vitamin C deficiency can result in scurvy. This condition presents with ecchymoses, perifollicular haemorrhages, and corkscrew hairs and purpura.

stem: A 78-year-old man asks you to look at a lesion on the right side of nose which has been getting slowly bigger over the past 2-3 months. On examination you observe a round, raised, flesh coloured lesion which is 3mm in diameter and has a central depression. The edges of the lesion appear rolled and contain some telangiectasia. What is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Basal cell carcinoma
The correct answer is Basal cell carcinoma. This is a type of nonmelanoma skin cancer, and it is the most common type of all skin cancers in the UK. The clinical features described in the question are highly suggestive of a nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC). BCCs often present as slow-growing, flesh-coloured or pink lesions with a pearly appearance. The rolled edges, central depression and presence of telangiectasia (dilated blood vessels) are classic features. They mostly occur on sun-exposed areas such as the face and neck.

Molluscum contagiosum
Molluscum contagiosum is an incorrect answer. It's a viral infection that presents with small, round, firm papules with a dimple or umbilication in the centre. However, these lesions are usually multiple and affect younger individuals rather than elderly patients.

Actinic keratosis
Actinic keratosis, also known as solar keratosis, is an incorrect answer. These are rough, scaly patches on sun-exposed skin which can be an early sign of skin cancer. However, they don't typically present with the rolled edges or central depression seen in this patient's lesion.

Squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is another type of non-melanoma skin cancer but it doesn't fit the description given in this case either. SCC typically presents as a firm, pink lump with a crusted surface and can rapidly increase in size - unlike the slow-growing lesion described here.

Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma is also incorrect because these types of cancers are usually present as pigmented lesions which change over time according to ABCDE rule (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6mm and Evolving nature). They do not have rolled edges or central depression like BCCs do.

stem: An 18-year-old female is reviewed in the dermatology clinic complaining of scalp hair loss. Which one of the following conditions is least likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda
The correct answer is Porphyria cutanea tarda. Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is a type of porphyria or a group of rare genetic disorders that affect the nervous system and skin. The main symptoms of PCT include blisters, itching, and swelling on the skin after exposure to sunlight. Hair loss is not typically associated with this condition, making it the least likely cause of scalp hair loss in this patient.

Discoid lupus
Discoid lupus, on the other hand, can indeed be associated with scalp hair loss. Discoid lupus erythematosus is a chronic skin condition characterised by inflamed, scaly and discoloured patches often found on the face, ears and scalp. In severe cases, these lesions can cause permanent hair loss due to scarring alopecia.

Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis is a common fungal infection that primarily affects children but can occur at any age. It affects the scalp leading to areas of scaling and hair loss. The fungi invade the hair shafts causing them to break off at the level of the scalp surface leaving behind bald patches.

Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disorder where the immune system attacks hair follicles resulting in non-scarring hair loss. It usually presents as one or several circular bald patches on the scalp or body.

Telogen effluvium
Telogen effluvium refers to temporary hair shedding often related to stress, illness or medication use. This condition results from a larger number of hairs than normal entering into 'telogen' phase - a resting stage in the natural life cycle of a hair follicle - leading to increased daily shedding and diffuse thinning across the whole scalp.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with anaemia. On further questioning, you find that he has a lifelong history of recurrent, severe nosebleeds and characteristic erythematous spots around his lips, which blanch when pressed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
The key is in the recognition of the telangiectasias, which are often found on the skin of the lips, nose and fingers. With this and the epistaxis, two of the three criteria to diagnose Hereditary Haemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT) are met. Anaemia is a common complaint in those with HHT. It is due to epistaxis or otherwise asymptomatic GI tract bleeding. Another finding could be hypoxia due to pulmonary arteriovenous malformations. The exact features vary, depending on where the arteriovenous malformations are located.

von Hippel-Lindau
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is caused by a faulty tumour suppressor gene resulting in the development of multiple unusual tumours including haemangioblastoma, phaeochromocytoma or renal cell carcinoma. At least two tumours must be present to make the diagnosis in someone without a family history (compared to just one when a family history is present).

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
Peutz Jeghers syndrome is a disorder causing large numbers of polyps in the intestine which become cancerous in a majority of patients. They have pigmented lesions around the lips which are not telangiectasia. There is no history of epistaxis.

Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis Type 1 is benign tumour disorder. Despite the nonmalignant nature of the tumours, they can have severe consequences depending on the location. Optic gliomas can lead to blindness, neurofibromas (found in the peripheral nervous system) can lead to learning disabilities and epilepsy. Other characteristic findings include caf-au-lait spots (flat, hyperpigmented, brown cutaneous lesions), axillary freckling, Lisch nodules (on the iris) and dermal neurofibromas (small, rubbery, cutaneous lumps).

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small- and medium-vessel vasculitis which primarily affects the sinuses, kidneys and lungs. Sinus dysfunction is the most common initial symptom causing nasal congestion or epistaxis. If a rash is present, it is usually made up of palpable purpura from small vessel inflammation.

stem: A 74-year-old woman develops tense, itchy blisters on her inner thighs and upper arms. Given the likely diagnosis, what will immunofluorescence of the skin biopsy demonstrate?
options: Loss of fibrinogen at the basement membrane
Granular IgG along the basement membrane
IgM crystallization at the dermal junctions
Linear IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction
IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction
explanation:
IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction
Bullous pemphigoid: immunofluorescence shows IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The correct answer is IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. This patient's presentation of tense, itchy blisters on the inner thighs and upper arms in an elderly woman is highly suggestive of bullous pemphigoid, which is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder in the elderly. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of skin biopsies in bullous pemphigoid characteristically shows linear deposits of IgG and complement component C3 along the dermoepidermal junction. These deposits represent autoantibodies directed against hemidesmosomal proteins (primarily BP180 and BP230) that are critical for epidermal-dermal adhesion. The binding of these autoantibodies leads to complement activation, inflammatory cell recruitment, and subsequent blister formation due to separation at the dermoepidermal junction.

Loss of fibrinogen at the basement membrane
Loss of fibrinogen at the basement membrane is not a characteristic finding in bullous pemphigoid or other primary blistering disorders. Fibrinogen deposition (rather than loss) may be seen in vasculitis or other inflammatory conditions affecting the skin, but it is not a diagnostic feature of autoimmune blistering diseases. Therefore, this answer is incorrect.

Granular IgG along the basement membrane
Granular IgG along the basement membrane is incorrect for bullous pemphigoid, which shows linear rather than granular deposits. Granular IgG deposits along the basement membrane are characteristic of lupus erythematosus, particularly discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus. This pattern, often referred to as the 'lupus band test,' represents immune complex deposition at the dermoepidermal junction but produces a different clinical picture than the tense blisters described in this case.

IgM crystallization at the dermal junctions
IgM crystallization at the dermal junctions is not a recognised immunofluorescence pattern in any common dermatological condition. IgM deposits may be seen in certain conditions such as dermatomyositis or lupus erythematosus, but they do not typically form crystalline structures at dermal junctions. This answer option is therefore incorrect and not consistent with any established immunofluorescence pattern in skin diseases.

Linear IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction
Linear IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction is characteristic of linear IgA disease (LAD), another autoimmune blistering disorder. While LAD can present with tense blisters, it is less common than bullous pemphigoid in elderly patients and often presents with a 'cluster of jewels' appearance of small blisters arranged in an annular pattern. LAD is distinguished from bullous pemphigoid by the presence of linear IgA (rather than IgG) deposits on immunofluorescence. While this pattern is seen in a blistering disorder, it does not match the most likely diagnosis in this elderly patient, which is bullous pemphigoid.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with a persistent erythematous rash on her cheeks and a 'red nose'. She describes occasional episodes of facial flushing. On examination erythematous skin is noted on the nose and cheeks associated with occasional papules. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Topical ivermectin
Rosacea: topical ivermectin is first-line for patients with mild papules and/or pustules. Given that this woman has mild symptoms, topical ivermectin should be used first line.

stem: A 46-year-old man is being investigated for recurrent episodes of melaena. He gives a history of nosebleeds, which occur frequently, almost every week. He is not aware of his family history, as he was adopted. Physical examination reveals telangiectasias over the lips and buccal mucosa. His blood tests are as follows: Hb 90 g/L (135 - 180) Platelets 250 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.0 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Ferritin 5 ng/mL (20 - 230) Reticulocytes 0.3 % (0.5 - 1.5) Peripheral blood film Microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
The correct answer is autosomal dominant. The patient's symptoms suggest a diagnosis of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, which is an autosomal dominant condition. This means that an affected individual has a 50% chance of passing the disorder to each of their offspring. HHT is characterized by multiple telangiectasias over the skin and mucous membranes, frequent nosebleeds (epistaxis), and visceral lesions such as gastrointestinal telangiectasias which can cause bleeding and result in iron deficiency anaemia, as seen in this patient. Despite being adopted and unaware of his family history, the combination of his symptoms strongly suggests HHT.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. Some bleeding disorders with an autosomal recessive inheritance include platelet function disorders like Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard-Soulier syndrome, and patients will generally exhibit petechiae or ecchymoses on examination.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial inheritance is incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is a non-Mendelian type of inheritance where the transmission is entirely through the maternal line. All the offspring of an affected mother will be affected, whereas the offspring of an affected father do not inherit the disease. Mitochondrial disorders mainly have neurological manifestations, and examples include MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke) and Leber optic atrophy.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect. These conditions are very rare and can be remembered using the mnemonic FAIR COX, where F - Fragile X syndrome, A - Alport's syndrome, I - Incontinentia pigmenti, R - Retts syndrome, C - Charcot Marie Tooth disease type X, O - Orofaciodigital syndrome, X- X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. Bleeding disorders inherited in an Xlinked recessive pattern include haemophilia A (due to factor VIII deficiency) and B (due to factor IX deficiency). These patients commonly have a history of ecchymoses and hematoma formation in their joints and soft tissues.

stem: A 67-year-old man who is a retired builder presents following the development of a number of red, scaly lesions on his left temple. These were initially small and flat but are now erythematous and rough to touch. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Actinic keratoses
The correct answer is actinic keratoses. Actinic keratoses are premalignant lesions that typically develop on sun-exposed areas of the skin, such as the face, scalp, and arms. These lesions are more common in older individuals with a history of significant sun exposure, like our patient who is a retired builder. The clinical presentation of actinic keratoses includes red, scaly patches that may be rough to touch.

Pityriasis versicolor
Pityriasis versicolor is an incorrect answer because it is a superficial fungal infection caused by Malassezia species and presents with hypo- or hyperpigmented macules on the trunk and upper extremities. The lesions are often covered with fine scales but are not typically erythematous or rough to touch.

Seborrhoeic keratosis
Seborrhoeic keratosis is also an incorrect answer. Although seborrhoeic keratoses can present as pigmented, scaly lesions, they are usually well-circumscribed and have a 'stuck-on' appearance. They are benign growths that commonly occur in older adults but do not share the same risk factors for malignant transformation as actinic keratoses.

Polymorphous light eruption
Polymorphous light eruption is another incorrect option. This condition refers to an abnormal immune response to sunlight exposure, resulting in the development of itchy papules or plaques on sun-exposed skin. However, polymorphous light eruption typically presents acutely after intense sun exposure rather than developing slowly over time like actinic keratoses.

Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma is an incorrect answer as well. Malignant melanoma is a type of skin cancer arising from melanocytes and may present with asymmetrical pigmented lesions that change in size or shape over time. While it is important to consider malignant melanoma in a patient with new skin lesions, the clinical presentation of erythematous, scaly patches is more consistent with actinic keratoses.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents to her GP with an itchy rash of several weeks' duration. She describes the rash as being present on her hands and around the elbows. She is otherwise well and has no past medical history except for hypertension. On examination, a papular, polygonal, violaceous, flat-topped rash is present on the palms, in her elbow creases and on the soles of her feet. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the first-line treatment?
explanation:
Topical clobetasol
Potent topical steroids are the first-line treatment for lichen planus. The diagnosis here is that of lichen planus, given the history and examination findings. In the first instance, a potent topical steroid should be used - and so topical clobetasol is the correct answer. Weaker steroids, such as hydrocortisone, are often ineffective.

Oral acitretin
Oral acitretin is incorrect. This is a retinoid, a second-line alternative to oral steroids if topical steroids are not effective. However, this patient should try topical steroids first.

Oral azathioprine
Oral azathioprine is incorrect - this is an immunosuppressant and comes with significant side effects of its own. This will be used in significant, refractory disease if other oral measures have failed.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is incorrect - this is a second-line option if topical steroids fail to control the rash.

Topical emollient
Topical emollients are incorrect. Whilst useful in alleviating itch and general symptoms, they will not help to resolve the disease.

stem: Which one of the following is least recognised as a cause of erythroderma in the UK?
explanation:
Lichen planus
Lichen planus is a non-infectious, inflammatory skin condition that typically affects the skin and oral mucosa. It can present with a variety of morphologies including papules, plaques, or erosions but erythroderma (generalised redness of the skin) is not a recognised feature.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma, specifically cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), can indeed cause erythroderma. This condition, also known as Sezary syndrome when it presents with erythroderma, leukemic involvement and lymphadenopathy, is rare but well-recognised.

Drug eruption
Drug eruption is another well-known cause of erythroderma. Certain medications can lead to severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) such as Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS), Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), all of which may present with erythroderma.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is one of the most common causes of erythroderma in the UK. In particular, uncontrolled plaque psoriasis can progress to erythrodermic psoriasis - an uncommon but severe variant characterised by widespread fiery redness covering most of the body surface area.

Eczema
Eczema, or more precisely atopic dermatitis, can also lead to erythroderma especially during severe flare-ups or if poorly controlled. This usually occurs in patients with a history of atopy who experience an intense inflammatory response that extends beyond localised areas to involve almost all body surfaces.

stem: A 19-year-old woman attends the dermatology clinic for severe nodulocystic acne, refractory to topical treatments and oral antibiotics. The decision is made to commence oral isotretinoin. She is sexually active and reports consistent use of the combined oral contraceptive pill. A pregnancy test is negative. What is the most appropriate advice regarding contraception?
options: Advise use of barrier methods in addition to the oral contraceptive pill
Continue the oral contraceptive pill as sole contraception
Stop the oral contraceptive pill and switch to a progesterone-only implant
Advise abstinence for one month before and after treatment
Perform monthly pregnancy tests during treatment
explanation:
Advise use of barrier methods in addition to the oral contraceptive pill
Advise use of barrier methods in addition to the oral contraceptive pill is the correct answer. Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen, and strict pregnancy prevention measures are mandatory. The UK's Pregnancy Prevention Programme (PPP) requires that a patient uses either at least one highly effective, user-independent method of contraception (e.g., an intrauterine device or a contraceptive implant) OR two complementary user-dependent forms. The combined oral contraceptive pill is a user-dependent method. As this patient is already established on the pill, the most appropriate and direct advice to meet the PPP criteria is to add a second complementary method, such as a barrier method (e.g., condoms).

Continue the oral contraceptive pill as sole contraception
Continue the oral contraceptive pill as sole contraception is incorrect. While the combined oral contraceptive pill is an effective method of contraception, it is user-dependent and has a 'typical-use' failure rate that is considered unacceptably high in the context of isotretinoin's teratogenicity. The PPP guidelines explicitly state that a single user-dependent method is insufficient.

Stop the oral contraceptive pill and switch to a progesterone-only implant
Stop the oral contraceptive pill and switch to a progesterone-only implant is a plausible but less appropriate option in this specific context. A progesterone-only implant is a highly effective, user-independent method and would be acceptable as a sole contraceptive agent. However, the patient is already established on the combined pill. The guidelines provide two equivalent options for meeting the safety criteria. Advising the addition of a barrier method is less disruptive for the patient than changing her established hormonal contraception and is an equally valid way to comply with the PPP.

Advise abstinence for one month before and after treatment
Advise abstinence for one month before and after treatment is incorrect. While total abstinence is an effective method of pregnancy prevention, this advice is incomplete. Contraception (or abstinence) must be maintained for one month before, for the entire duration of treatment, and for one month after stopping isotretinoin. This option omits the crucial period during treatment. For a sexually active patient, advising on effective contraception is the standard approach.

Perform monthly pregnancy tests during treatment
Perform monthly pregnancy tests during treatment is incorrect. Although monthly pregnancy testing is a mandatory component of monitoring under the PPP, it is not a form of contraception. The question specifically asks for advice regarding contraception. Pregnancy testing is a safety check to ensure the primary contraceptive measures have not failed; it does not prevent pregnancy from occurring.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with known polycystic ovary syndrome presents with excessive hair growth of the chest, back and face. She reports her symptoms first developed around the time of puberty, with the hair continuing to remain prominent, growing back despite removal via waxing and shaving. The underlying skin is normal and the patient is otherwise well with no other medical conditions. What topical agent is the treatment of choice for the facial features of this patient's condition?
explanation:
Eflornithine
Topical eflornithine is the treatment of choice for facial hirsutism, blocking putrescine, an organic compound required for hair follicle growth and inhibiting cellular proliferation.

Benzoyl peroxide
Benzoyl peroxide is one of the first-line treatments for the common dermatological condition acne. It is thought to reduce the production of sebum from the skin sebaceous glands, reducing the formation of comedo (clogged hair follicles) and inhibiting Cutibacterium acnes, the main bacterium associated with acne. Benzoyl peroxide plays no role in the management of facial hirsutism.

Clobetasone
Clobetasone is a topical corticosteroid used in the management of several dermatological inflammatory conditions such as eczema, psoriasis and other forms of dermatitis. Corticosteroids do not play a significant role in the management of hirsutism.

Ethinylestradiol
Ethinylestradiol is an oestrogen medication used in several combined oral contraceptive pills (OCP). Although OCPs are used in the management of hirsutism, ethinylestradiol is an oral medication, not topical, and it must be used in a combined formula with a progestin medication.

Retinoid
Retinoids are a form of vitamin A and is used in inflammatory skin disorders, mainly severe acne when first-line medications have failed. Retinoids inhibit inflammatory pathways and specific cell proliferation involved in dermatological conditions but again it has no role in the management of facial hirsutism.

stem: An 84-year-old woman with a history of ischaemic heart disease is reviewed in the dermatology clinic. Her current medication includes aspirin, simvastatin, bisoprolol, ramipril and isosorbide mononitrate. She has developed tense blistering lesions on her legs. Each lesion is around 1 to 3 cm in diameter and she reports that they are slightly pruritic. Examination of her mouth and vulva is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bullous pemphigoid
Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disorder that commonly affects elderly patients. It presents with tense, pruritic blisters on the skin, often on the extremities, and typically spares mucosal surfaces like the mouth and vulva. The patient's age, presence of tense blisters, and lack of mucosal involvement make bullous pemphigoid the most likely diagnosis in this scenario.

Pemphigus
Pemphigus is another autoimmune blistering disorder; however, it typically presents with flaccid blisters and erosions involving both the skin and mucosal surfaces. The absence of mucosal involvement and tense nature of the blisters make pemphigus less likely than bullous pemphigoid.

Drug reaction to aspirin
A drug reaction to aspirin could potentially cause a cutaneous eruption; however, drug reactions usually present with a more diffuse rash rather than localized tense blisters. Additionally, the patient has been taking aspirin as part of her medication regimen without any previous issues mentioned.

Epidermolysis bullosa
Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited disorders characterized by skin fragility and blister formation following minor trauma. Given the patient's age and lack of history suggesting skin fragility or recurrent blistering throughout her life, this diagnosis is unlikely.

Scabies
Scabies is a parasitic infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei. It typically presents with intense pruritus and a papular rash affecting primarily interdigital spaces, wrists, axillae, waistline and genital areas. The presentation of tense blisters on the legs without other typical features makes scabies an unlikely diagnosis for this patient.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic with areas of hypopigmentation on her shoulders and back. Her spouse noted these as the lesions did not tan during a recent holiday to Spain. This is her first episode. She is worried as she is immunosuppressed with prednisolone and azathioprine following a renal transplant. On examination, there are crops of slightly scaly, coalescing patches on her shoulders and upper back. There is no erythema or induration. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Topical ketoconazole
Topical ketoconazole is the correct answer. This woman has pityriasis versicolor, which is a superficial fungal infection (Malassezia) that leads to hypopigmented macular lesions on seborrhoeic regions of the trunk. It is most common in the summer months, and a common feature is a relapsing disease. Long-term systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressant use increases the risk of infection. It is primarily a clinical diagnosis that can be easily treated with topical antifungals, such as ketoconazole. Systemic therapy is reserved for extensive disease. In this patient, prophylactic treatment should be considered once this current episode is successfully treated.

Do nothing
Do nothing is incorrect. The physical appearance of pityriasis versicolor can be distressing to some, and given the fact it can be a relapsing disease, treatment should be offered. In this case, that would be in the form of a ketoconazole shampoo.

Oral itraconazole
Oral itraconazole is incorrect. Oral antifungals are reserved for the treatment of lesions that are extensive and resistant to topical therapy. It can sometimes be considered first-line treatment in those who are immunosuppressed and who experience frequent relapses, but this is the first episode for this woman.

Phototherapy
Phototherapy is incorrect. In patients with hypopigmented pityriasis versicolor, the resulting dyschromia can be long-lasting, even after eradication. UV phototherapy should be considered after complete eradication of the fungus, not before.

Topical steroids
Topical steroids is incorrect. Topical steroids have no role in the treatment of pityriasis versicolor.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a one-week history of a rash. He has recently returned from a holiday in Spain. He does not have any significant past medical history and does not take any regular medications. On examination, there is a rash affecting his trunk, consisting of multiple hypopigmented patches, which are slightly scaly. Based on the likely diagnosis, what is the appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Topical ketoconazole
Ketoconazole shampoo is used to treat pityriasis versicolor. Topical ketoconazole is correct. A rash consisting of multiple hypopigmented patches affecting the trunk is a typical description of pityriasis versicolor. The rash may be more visible in those with a suntan, which we might expect this man to have after returning from a holiday in Spain. The treatment in the first instance is topical ketoconazole.

Oral itraconazole
Oral itraconazole is incorrect. This is used in disease refractory to initial treatment.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is incorrect. Again, oral steroids are indicated in a wide variety of inflammatory skin conditions but they are not indicated in this disease.

Topical betamethasone
Topical betamethasone is incorrect. Topical steroids are used in a wide variety of skin conditions including eczema and psoriasis. However, they are not indicated in pityriasis versicolor.

Vitamin D analogue
Vitamin D analogue is incorrect. This class of medication is used in the treatment of psoriasis, not pityriasis versicolor.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with a history of learning difficulties is reviewed in clinic. She is known to have erythema ab igne on her legs but according to her carer still spends long hours in front of her electric fire. Which one of the following skin lesions is she at risk of developing?
options: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma of the skin
explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma
The correct answer is Squamous cell carcinoma. Erythema ab igne is a skin condition characterized by a reticulated, erythematous, and hyperpigmented appearance caused by prolonged exposure to moderate heat. Chronic exposure to heat can lead to epidermal changes, including atypia and dysplasia. These changes may predispose an individual to the development of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), which arises from the keratinocytes in the epidermis. SCC is the second most common type of skin cancer and is more likely to occur in areas of chronic inflammation or injury.

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma of the skin
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma of the skin is an incorrect answer as this condition is not associated with erythema ab igne or exposure to heat sources. Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas are a group of non-Hodgkin lymphomas that primarily affect the skin, with mycosis fungoides being the most common subtype. The exact cause is unknown, but it is thought to involve genetic and environmental factors.

Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is also an incorrect answer because it has no known association with erythema ab igne or chronic heat exposure. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is a rare, slow-growing dermal neoplasm that arises from fibroblasts. It typically presents as a firm, raised nodule on the trunk or extremities and has a high local recurrence rate after surgical removal.

Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is another incorrect option as it does not have a direct link with erythema ab igne or chronic heat exposure. BCC arises from basal cells in the epidermis and is the most common type of skin cancer. Risk factors for BCC include ultraviolet light exposure, fair skin, and a history of ionizing radiation.

Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma is also an incorrect answer because it is not associated with erythema ab igne or heat exposure. Malignant melanoma arises from the melanocytes in the epidermis and is the most aggressive form of skin cancer. Risk factors include excessive sun exposure, family history, and the presence of atypical moles.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is reviewed. She presented 4 weeks ago with itchy dry skin on her arms and was diagnosed as having atopic eczema. She was prescribed hydrocortisone 1% cream with an emollient. Unfortunately there has been no improvement in her symptoms. What is the next step in management, alongside continued regular use of an emollient?
explanation:
Clobetasone butyrate 0.05%
Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% is a moderately potent topical steroid and would be the most suitable next step in management. It is important to note the potency difference between two very similar sounding steroids - Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% (moderate) and Clobetasol propionate 0.05% (very potent)

Betamethasone valerate 0.1%
Betamethasone valerate 0.1% is a potent topical steroid, but a moderately potent steroid like Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% is more suitable as the next step in management.

Clobetasol propionate 0.05%
Clobetasol propionate 0.05% is a very potent topical steroid and is not the most suitable next step in management for this patient.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presented at 15-weeks gestation with a 1-week history of erythematous, tender lesions on the pretibial aspects of both legs. The patient reported having had a 'flu-like' illness with fever, a sore throat and dry cough during the same time as these lesions developing. The 'flu' symptoms resolved within 10 days without medical intervention, but the lesions on her legs persisted. An initial antistreptolysin-O titre was raised. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum can be caused by streptococcal infection. Erythema nodosum is a condition that causes painful red bumps under the skin on the shins. It is one of the most common forms of panniculitis that causes inflammation of the subcutaneous fat under the skin. Erythema nodosum can occur in pregnancy due to hormonal changes and infectious with streptococcal pharyngitis being a common cause as described here.

Erythema ab igne
Erythema ab igne is a skin reaction caused by chronic exposure to infrared radiation in the form of heat and is not commonly seen as a direct result of pregnancy.

Erythema gyratum repens
Erythema gyratum repens is a rare paraneoplastic type of annular erythema with a distinctive figurate wood-grain appearance which has a strong association with malignancy.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction usually triggered by infections, most commonly herpes simplex virus (HSV) and can be associated with pregnancy. However, it appears as target-like patches (dark circles with purple-grey centres) which are not described here.

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is a relatively common skin disorder that can occur in women during pregnancy. It usually presents within the first pregnancy. It appears as an itchy, bumpy rash that starts in the stretch marks of the abdomen in the last 3 months of pregnancy then clears with delivery. This is unlikely to be the case here.

stem: A 24-year-old student presents due to some lesions on his lower abdomen. These have been present for the past six weeks. Initially, there was one lesion but since that time more lesions have appeared. On examination around 10 lesions are seen; they are raised, around 1-2mm in diameter and have an umbilicated appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Molluscum contagiosum
The correct answer is Molluscum contagiosum. This viral infection, caused by a poxvirus, characteristically presents with multiple dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. The clinical scenario perfectly describes the typical presentation: multiple small (1-2mm) raised lesions with an umbilicated appearance, which spread over time from a single lesion. The condition is common in children and young adults, and can be sexually transmitted in adults. The lesions typically persist for 6-12 months before spontaneously resolving.

Genital warts
Genital warts are caused by Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and typically present as flesh-coloured papules with a rough, cauliflower-like appearance. They do not show umbilication and are usually found in the anogenital region. While they can spread, they don't typically present with the smooth, dome-shaped appearance described in this case.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus presents with purple, polygonal, pruritic papules and plaques, often with a white lacy pattern (Wickham's striae) visible on their surface. The lesions are typically larger than 1-2mm and lack umbilication. They commonly affect the flexor surfaces of wrists, legs, and oral mucosa.

Keratosis pilaris
Keratosis pilaris presents as multiple small, rough follicular papules, typically on the upper arms, thighs, and cheeks. These lesions are associated with dry skin, appear as 'chicken skin', and do not show umbilication. They are typically symmetrical and present from childhood.

Folliculitis
Folliculitis is an inflammation of hair follicles, presenting as small, red, tender pustules centred on hair follicles. The lesions are typically inflamed and may be painful or itchy, unlike the painless, flesh-coloured lesions described in this case. They also tend to resolve more quickly and don't show the characteristic umbilication seen in molluscum contagiosum.

stem: A 24-year-old woman attends with an intensely itchy rash over her buttocks and knees. She also complains of bloating, and diarrhoea. On examination, you note vesicular skin lesions over the elbows, knees, and buttocks. What would you expect to see on a skin biopsy?
options: IgA deposition in the subcutaneous fat
explanation:
IgA deposition in the dermis
Dermatitis herpetiformis - caused by IgA deposition in the dermis. The clinical features are suggestive of dermatitis herpetiformis with coexistent coeliac disease. This disorder is characterised by intensely itchy, vesicular skin lesions on the extensor surfaces (e.g. elbows, knees, buttocks). IgA deposition in the dermis is correct. A skin biopsy remains the gold standard for the diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates the deposition of IgA in a granular pattern in the upper dermis.

stem: A 7-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his family. He has a history of eczema, which is usually well-controlled, and previous chickenpox. Over the last 5 days, he has developed a worsening rash. This started with clusters of blisters on the face and neck. These have now spread to the trunk and arms. You find a symmetrical monomorphic eruption of small blisters with central umbilication. They are filled with yellow fluid and blood-stained. The skin surrounding these clusters is normal. The patient is febrile and lethargic. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Herpes simplex virus
Eczema herpeticum is a primary infection of the skin caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and uncommonly coxsackievirus. This patient's presentation is suggestive of eczema herpeticum. This affects patients with atopic eczema and typically presents with clusters of blisters, fever, and malaise. The lesions may have clear, yellow, or purulent fluid and are often bloodstained. Central umbilication is common. Herpes simplex virus is the most common cause, although in some cases others such as coxsackievirus may be seen.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. This is a common cause of skin and soft tissue infections in adults and children. In children, it can be associated with outbreaks of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. This does cause a widespread rash but is generally quite different to that described here, with wrinkling of the skin followed by the development of large fluid-filled blisters which rupture easily. A generalised exfoliative dermatitis is seen. In the case described, the normal skin between lesions makes this less likely, as does the description of small umbilicated blisters rather than large bullae.

Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus pyogenes is incorrect. This is a frequent cause of infections in children, including pharyngitis and impetigo. It can cause secondary infections in patients with eczema herpeticum, generally presenting as cellulitis spreading from the lesions. In this case, we are told the skin between lesions is normal, making this less likely.

Trichophyton rubrum
Trichophyton rubrum is incorrect. This is a common cause of fungal skin infections such as tinea corporis. This typically presents with a single circular patch with erythema and scaling. Multiple lesions can develop and may coalesce but generally would not spread as widely as described. It is also generally asymmetrical.

Varicella zoster virus
