Varicella zoster virus is incorrect. This is the causative organism of two distinct diseases, chickenpox and shingles. The blisters of chickenpox can be difficult to distinguish from eczema herpeticum. In chickenpox, the blisters do tend to be larger and have larger spaces between them. In this case, the history of eczema puts the patient at higher risk of eczema herpeticum. The key clue is the previous history of chickenpox - it is extremely unusual to have this illness more than once.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with a several-month history of lesions on the face. He has a past medical history of recurrent epistaxis since childhood. He is unaware of his biological family history, having been adopted at birth. On examination, numerous telangiectasias are noted on the face, lips, tongue and inside the mouth. He is subsequently referred to specialists for further investigations: Endoscopy Several telangiectasias in the stomach and duodenum CT chest, abdomen and pelvis Numerous hepatic arteriovenous malformations What is the mode of inheritance of the underlying condition?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia - autosomal dominant This patient's presentation is suggestive of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome. This is characterised by telangiectasia over the skin and mucous membranes, epistaxis and visceral lesions (such as the gastrointestinal telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations seen here). The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, although in this case, the patient does not know of his biological family history.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. HHT is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Autosomal recessive conditions include cystic fibrosis and thalassaemia.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial is incorrect. Mitochondrial conditions are generally rare. As mitochondrial DNA is inherited solely from the mother, diseases are also passed from mother to child. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is a rare condition associated with mitochondrial inheritance.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect. Examples of such conditions include Vitamin D-resistant rickets and most cases of Alport syndrome. HHT, however, is autosomal dominant.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. Examples of these conditions include haemophilia A and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to his GP with an area of multiple circular, depressed ulcerating lesions each measuring 1-3mm around his chin/neck region which his parent first noticed the day before. The child is otherwise well and the GP prescribes a topical emollient for a possible flare of his known atopic eczema. Two days later the child is brought back in as the rash had increased in size and they have now developed diarrhoea and a fever. What is the most appropriate treatment to commence?
explanation:
Arrange admission for IV aciclovir
Eczema herpeticum is a serious condition that requires IV antivirals. This child has presented with the classic progression of eczema herpeticum where a disrupted skin barrier, often secondary to another condition such as atopic eczema, is infected by herpes simplex virus 1 or 2. Coxsackievirus A16 or vaccinia virus can also cause the infection. The condition presents with a rapidly increasing rash along with other symptoms including fever, lymphadenopathy and bowel changes. Eczema herpeticum is a severe, disseminating infection that can progress to multiple end-organ-failure rapidly and therefore requires IV aciclovir urgently if suspected.

Arrange admission for IV hydrocortisone
IV hydrocortisone can be used in the management of several inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. However, they have a limited role in the treatment of infections and may potentially increase the progression of eczema herpeticum due to immunosuppression.

Oral prednisolone & antihistamine
Oral prednisolone & antihistamine are commonly used in combination for some inflammatory skin conditions but do not play a role in the management of infections such as eczema herpeticum.

Topical 1% hydrocortisone cream
A topical 1% hydrocortisone cream can be used for inflammatory conditions such as eczema and contact dermatitis. However, topical steroids do not play a role in the management of eczema herpeticum.

Topical fusidic acid
Fusidic acid is an antibiotic used in topical form for the treatment of infections of the skin or eyes. As an antibiotic, it generally is only effective against bacterial infections such as Streptococcus or Staphylococcus species and therefore does not have a role in the management of eczema herpeticum.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of Parkinson's disease presents due to the development of an itchy, red rash on his neck, behind his ears and around the nasolabial folds. He had a similar flare up last winter but did not seek medical attention. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Parkinson's disease is associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis. This condition is a common, chronic or relapsing form of eczema/dermatitis that primarily affects sebum-gland rich areas including the scalp, face, and trunk. The presentation of an itchy, red rash on the neck, behind the ears and around the nasolabial folds in this patient is highly suggestive of Seborrhoeic dermatitis. Notably, Parkinson's disease patients have a higher incidence of seborrhoeic dermatitis due to increased sebum production.

Levodopa associated dermatitis
Levodopa associated dermatitis is incorrect as it typically presents as xerosis (dry skin) and pruritus without a distinct rash. It would also likely affect other parts of the body rather than being localised to sebum-rich areas.

Flexural psoriasis
Flexural psoriasis is not correct because this type of psoriasis usually affects skin folds such as those found in the axillae or groin. It generally does not affect the face or scalp which are commonly involved in seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Acne rosacea
The option Acne rosacea is incorrect because rosacea typically presents with transient or persistent erythema, papules, pustules and telangiectasia on the face. Furthermore, rosacea does not cause itching which was one of the symptoms described by this patient.

Fixed drug reaction to ropinirole
A Fixed drug reaction to ropinirole, used in Parkinson's disease treatment, is unlikely because fixed drug reactions usually present as well-defined erythematous patches or plaques that recur at exactly the same site with each exposure to the drug. This patient had flare-ups during winter which suggests a seasonal influence rather than a constant exposure to medication.

stem: A 54-year-old man is referred by his GP to the dermatology outpatient department due to a facial rash which has persisted for the past 12 months. On examination there is a symmetrical rash consisting of extensive pustules and papules which affects his nose, cheeks and forehead. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Oral doxycycline + topical ivermectin
Rosacea: a combination of topical ivermectin + oral doxycycline is first-line for patients with severe papules and/or pustules. This patient's presentation is consistent with rosacea, specifically papulopustular (type 2) rosacea. According to NICE guidelines, the firstline treatment for moderate to severe papulopustular rosacea is oral tetracyclines (such as doxycycline) combined with topical therapy. Ivermectin 1% cream has shown superior efficacy compared to other topical agents and is now recommended as a first-line topical treatment. This combination therapy addresses both the inflammatory and antimicrobial aspects of the condition.

Topical metronidazole
Topical metronidazole alone would be insufficient for moderate to severe rosacea. While it is an appropriate topical agent for mild cases, this patient's extensive involvement would require systemic therapy. Metronidazole gel is more suitable as monotherapy for mild cases or as an adjunct to oral therapy.

Oral isotretinoin
Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe cases of rosacea that have failed to respond to conventional therapy with oral antibiotics and topical treatments. It would be inappropriate as a first-line treatment due to its significant side effect profile and the need for careful monitoring.

Oral hydroxychloroquine
Oral hydroxychloroquine is not indicated for rosacea. It is primarily used in autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. There is no evidence base for its use in rosacea, and it would not address the underlying pathophysiology of the condition.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone would be an inappropriate choice as systemic corticosteroids can actually worsen rosacea and lead to a steroid-induced rosacea-like condition. Corticosteroids can cause rebound flares and potentially aggravate the underlying condition. They should be avoided in rosacea unless there are specific indications such as severe inflammatory episodes requiring short-term use.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a rash affecting her cheeks, nose, and forehead. The rash is worse when exposed to the sun. She has no past medical history. On examination, there is an erythematous rash affecting her nose, cheeks, and forehead diffusely and involving the nasolabial folds. There is a minimal amount of papules and pustules visible. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the first-line treatment?
explanation:
Topical ivermectin
Topical ivermectin is correct. The patient presents with an erythematous rash along with papules/pustules affecting her nose, cheeks, and forehead. This is typical of rosacea. The first line of management in mild/moderate cases is topical ivermectin. The underlying aetiology of rosacea is complex and yet to be entirely elucidated. There is a probable multifactorial aetiology to the disease including immune and vascular dysfunction, neurogenic dysregulation, presence of cutaneous microorganisms, ultraviolet damage, and skin barrier dysfunction. Ivermectin is postulated to have an anti-inflammatory and anti-parasitic effect, targeting cutaneous organisms like Demodex mites.

Oral doxycycline
Oral doxycycline is incorrect. This can be used in combination with topical ivermectin in severe cases of rosacea. It has anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic properties that make it useful in the treatment of rosacea.

Oral hydroxychloroquine
Oral hydroxychloroquine is incorrect. This is an anti-malarial used in the management of systemic lupus erythematosus. It can be used for the skin manifestations of the disease. Malar rash affecting the cheeks and nose in lupus tends to spare the nasolabial folds, which are involved in this case.

Oral lymecycline
Oral lymecycline is incorrect. This is an option for the treatment of acne. However, erythema in acne tends to be local to the papules/pustules rather than diffusely affecting a wider area like in rosacea. Therefore, rosacea is the more likely diagnosis in this case.

Topical steroids
Topical steroids are incorrect. This can be used for a wide variety of inflammatory skin disorders (although should be minimised on the face where possible). It is not the first-line treatment of rosacea, which is the most likely diagnosis here.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents for the removal of a mole. Where on the body are keloid scars most likely to form?
explanation:
Sternum
Keloid scars are most common on the sternum. The correct answer is the sternum. Keloid scars are a result of an overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue that usually develops after the healing of a skin injury. The scar extends beyond the borders of the original wound, does not regress and tends to recur after excision. The sternum, along with other areas such as shoulders, upper arms and earlobes, is particularly prone to keloid formation due to high tension in these areas.

Lower back
The lower back, although it can develop keloid scars, is not as commonly affected as the sternum. This may be due to less tension in this area compared to the chest wall or less frequent injury.

Abdomen
Keloids can also form on the abdomen, but they are not as common in this location as on the sternum. It's important to note that surgical incisions, such as those for abdominal surgeries, can lead to keloid formation if the individual has a predisposition.

Flexor surfaces of limbs
The flexor surfaces of limbs are less likely to form keloids compared to other parts of the body because these areas are usually covered by clothing and therefore protected from trauma. However, piercings or burns in these areas could potentially lead to keloid formation.

Scalp
While it's possible for keloids to develop on the scalp, they're relatively rare in this location. This could be due to several factors including fewer injuries occurring on this part of the body or perhaps related to differences in hair follicle biology which may influence wound healing and scar formation.

stem: A 68-year-old female presents to her primary healthcare provider with the complaints of painful blisters on the gingival and buccal mucosa and skin that rupture easily and cause ulcers. The oral blisters started two months ago and the cutaneous lesions just a week ago. She has a history of hypertension, vitiligo and diabetes mellitus type 2. Examination of the oral cavity and the skin reveals scattered shallow ulcerations 8 mm to 1 cm in diameter. Biopsy of the lesions showed acantholysis. She has been started on corticosteroids. Which of the following is the most likely aetiology of the condition in this patient?
explanation:
Antibodies against desmoglein 3
Antibodies against desmoglein 3 are seen in pemphigus vulgaris. The sign and symptoms along with biopsy findings in the scenario are suggestive of pemphigus vulgaris. Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disease caused by antibodies directed against desmoglein 3, a cadherin-type epithelial cell adhesion molecule.

Antibodies against desmoplakin I
Antibodies against desmoplakin I are seen in paraneoplastic pemphigus.

Antibodies against desmoplakin II
Antibodies against desmoplakin II are also seen in paraneoplastic pemphigus.

Antibodies against desmocollin 1
Antibodies against desmocollin 1 are found in subcorneal pustular dermatosis type of IgA pemphigus.

Antibodies against desmoglein 1
Antibodies against desmoglein 1 are formed in pemphigus variants such as pemphigus foliaceous, pemphigus erythematosus and fogo selvagem.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is least likely to be associated with pyoderma gangrenosum?
explanation:
Syphilis
The correct answer is Syphilis. Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare, ulcerative cutaneous condition of unknown aetiology. It's frequently associated with systemic diseases, most commonly inflammatory bowel disease (such as Ulcerative colitis), haematological disorders (like Lymphoma and IgA monoclonal gammopathy) and rheumatologic conditions including Rheumatoid arthritis. However, there are no known associations between PG and Syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is one of the most common conditions associated with PG. Approximately 10-15% of individuals with PG also have ulcerative colitis. The exact pathogenesis is unclear but it's believed that shared immunopathogenic mechanisms might be responsible.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma, specifically non-Hodgkin lymphoma, has been reported to be associated with PG in numerous case reports. The link between these two conditions remains unclear but it's thought that aberrant immune response plays a key role.

IgA monoclonal gammopathy
IgA monoclonal gammopathy is another condition that has been linked with PG. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) can precede or follow the diagnosis of PG. It's hypothesised that abnormal IgA antibodies trigger an inflammatory response leading to the development of PG.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis has also been reported in association with PG. It's suggested that shared autoimmune pathways may contribute to this association although the exact mechanism remains elusive.

stem: A 60-year-old man is admitted to hospital with acute pneumonia. He has a past medical history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, alcohol excess and hypertension, and has been homeless for the last 12 years. On the post-take ward round, you notice that he has a brown-red discolouration of his face, neck, forearms and lower legs, with scaling and cracking of the skin. He complains that he is struggling to eat and drink and has persistent vomiting and diarrhoea. He seems a little disorientated. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely to be causing these symptoms?
explanation:
B3 (niacin)
Deficiency of niacin (B3) causes pellagra. The patient has some of the symptoms of pellagra, which is classically characterised by the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. The 'dementia' more commonly presents subtly with low mood, irritability, apathy and anxiety, progressing to delusions, psychosis, drowsiness and coma.

stem: A 7-year-old child is admitted to hospital after presenting with a rapidly progressing, painful rash. The child was previously well. The child's only past medical history includes asthma and eczema. The patient's regular medications are a salbutamol inhaler with a spacer, and topical emollients. There is no significant family history. On examination, monomorphic punched-out erosions are noted by the doctor. Which of the following is recognised as a common cause of this condition?
explanation:
Herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2
Eczema herpeticum is a primary infection of the skin caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and uncommonly coxsackievirus. The history and examination points towards a diagnosis of eczema herpeticum, which requires admission for treatment with intravenous aciclovir. The correct answer here is herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2. Less commonly, it can be caused by coxsackievirus A16.

Herpes simplex viruses 3 and 4
Herpes simplex viruses 3 and 4 do not exist.

Human herpesviruses 3 and 4
Human herpesviruses 3 and 4 are varicella-zoster virus and Epstein-Barr virus respectively. The former causes chickenpox, and the latter is implicated in several diseases, including infectious mononucleosis.

Human herpesviruses 6 and 8
Human herpesviruses 6 and 8 are incorrect - the former is implicated in several diseases, including the childhood illness roseola infantum, and the latter causes Kaposi's sarcoma.

Human papillomaviruses 6 and 11
Human papillomaviruses 6 and 11 are incorrect - these are common causes of genital warts (unlike 16 and 18, which are strongly linked to cervical cancer).

stem: A 4-year-old boy with a history of severe atopic eczema is brought to the emergency department. He has a 2-day history of a rapidly spreading, painful rash on his face and trunk. On examination, he is febrile and distressed. There are widespread, monomorphic, circular, punched-out erosions with some haemorrhagic crusting over affected areas. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
explanation:
Intravenous aciclovir
The clinical presentation is classic for eczema herpeticum, a dermatological emergency caused by disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in a patient with a preexisting skin condition, most commonly atopic eczema. The key features are the rapid onset of a painful rash in a patient with eczema, systemic symptoms such as fever, and the characteristic rash morphology of monomorphic, 'punched-out' erosions. This condition can lead to systemic viraemia and can be life-threatening or sight-threatening if there is ocular involvement. UK guidelines recommend immediate hospital admission and treatment with intravenous aciclovir to control viral replication and prevent complications.

Oral flucloxacillin
Oral flucloxacillin would be the treatment for impetigo, which is a common secondary bacterial infection in atopic eczema. Impetigo typically presents with golden, crusted lesions rather than the monomorphic, punched-out erosions described here. While secondary bacterial infection with Staphylococcus or Streptococcus can co-exist with eczema herpeticum, and antibiotics may be required as an adjunct, the primary, life-threatening pathology is the viral infection. Therefore, treating only the potential bacterial component would be inadequate and dangerous.

Topical hydrocortisone
Topical hydrocortisone is used to manage flares of atopic eczema by reducing inflammation. However, applying topical steroids to an active viral skin infection like eczema herpeticum is contraindicated. Steroids suppress the local immune response, which can lead to more extensive and severe viral replication, worsening the condition significantly. The presence of systemic features like fever also points towards a diagnosis beyond a simple eczema flare.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is reserved for severe, widespread flares of atopic eczema that are unresponsive to topical treatments. Similar to topical steroids, systemic corticosteroids are immunosuppressive and would be extremely dangerous in the context of a disseminated viral infection. This could lead to fulminant viraemia and multi-organ involvement. The clinical features in the stem are highly suggestive of infection rather than a primary inflammatory flare, making this an inappropriate and hazardous choice.

Intravenous flucloxacillin
Intravenous flucloxacillin would be indicated for a severe bacterial skin and soft tissue infection, such as cellulitis or staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS). However, the rash described does not fit with these diagnoses. Cellulitis presents as diffuse, poorly demarcated erythema and swelling, while SSSS involves widespread blistering and exfoliation. Although bacterial superinfection can occur in eczema herpeticum, the primary driver is the HSV infection, which must be treated with antiviral therapy urgently.

stem: A 35-year-old man attends his GP with an increasingly painful blistering lesion on his left leg. Initially, the lesion started as a small red bump but eventually progressed into a large ulcer. He was recently discharged from the hospital following an exacerbation of ulcerative colitis but is recovering well. On examination, there is a large erosive ulcer over the left medial aspect of his calf extending to the dorsal aspect of his foot. It is poorly defined and purple. Clinically his observations are stable. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the first-line management for this patient?
explanation:
Oral prednisolone
Oral steroids are the first-line treatment for pyoderma gangrenosum. Oral prednisolone is the correct answer. The patient in this vignette has pyoderma gangrenosum. This typically presents initially with a small blood blister or red bump before progressing to a large deep violaceous ulcer, commonly affecting the lower limbs. The patient's background of ulcerative colitis is also a clue to the diagnosis, given inflammatory bowel disease can predispose patients to developing pyoderma gangrenosum. Patients are often treated initially with oral prednisolone.

Oral ciclosporin
Oral cyclosporin is incorrect. This is an immunomodulating agent that can be given for treating pyoderma gangrenosum however, it is not first-line management. This patient has not trialled any treatment for his diagnosis yet, and the question specifically asks for the first-line management of the likely diagnosis. Oral cyclosporin is given if patients poorly respond to oral prednisolone.

Oral flucloxacillin
Oral flucloxacillin is incorrect. Oral flucloxacillin is the first line for bacterial skin infections such as cellulitis. There is no indication that this patient has a bacterial infection due to the absence of systemic features such as pyrexia, and lethargy, but also the absence of extensive erythema, oozing, and warmth over the affected region. Pyoderma gangrenosum is non-infectious, and as this patient does not have any features to suggest co-existing bacterial skin infection oral flucloxacillin would not be indicated.

Oral pentoxifylline
Oral pentoxifylline is incorrect. Oral pentoxifylline is an oral vasodilator that is specifically given in venous ulceration to improve the healing rate. Typically venous ulceration is large, shallow, and irregular with a granulating/exudative base seen over the gaiter or medial malleolus region. The presentation described in this scenario is not characterised by venous ulceration as the ulcer is deep, and purple and the patient does not have a background of risk factors predisposed to venous disease such as smoking, obesity and varicose veins. The description of a small blood blister developing into a deep violaceous ulcer on a background of ulcerative colitis points more to a diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum, and the treatment for this is oral steroids as described above.

Topical Dermovate
Topical Dermovate is incorrect. Topical dermovate is a potent topical steroid rarely given for skin conditions. Some indications for topical dermovate include chronic discoid lupus erythematosus, lichen simplex, hypertrophic lichen planus, and palmoplantar pustulosis. Although topical steroids can be given in mild, and local cases of pyoderma gangrenosum, this patient has an extension of his disease across the majority of his left leg, therefore oral prednisolone would be more appropriate to ensure sufficient, successful treatment of the condition and prevention of relapse.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to the dermatology clinic with a 2-week history of multiple tender, erythematous nodules over both shins. She is otherwise well with no other symptoms. On examination, there are several warm, raised, red nodules on the anterior aspects of her lower legs, consistent with erythema nodosum. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation:
Chest X-ray
Chest x-ray should be done in all patients with erythema nodosum. Erythema nodosum is a reactive panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat) and is often a cutaneous marker of an underlying systemic disease. While many cases are idiopathic, it is crucial to investigate for common and serious underlying causes. A chest X-ray is the single most important initial investigation in all patients presenting with erythema nodosum. This is because it can reveal evidence of sarcoidosis (typically bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy), tuberculosis, or, less commonly, lymphoma. Sarcoidosis is one of the most common identifiable causes of erythema nodosum in adults. Identifying these conditions early is critical for patient management and prognosis. Therefore, regardless of the presence or absence of respiratory symptoms, a chest X-ray is a mandatory first step.

Anti-streptolysin O titre
Anti-streptolysin O titre is an incorrect choice for the most appropriate initial investigation. While Group A streptococcal pharyngitis is a very common trigger for erythema nodosum, particularly in children and young adults, it is more important to first exclude the more serious intrathoracic pathologies like sarcoidosis and tuberculosis. The ASO titre or a throat swab can be part of the subsequent workup, especially if there is a recent history of a sore throat, but the chest X-ray takes precedence due to the severity of the conditions it can help diagnose. In an asymptomatic patient, prioritising the exclusion of sarcoidosis or TB is standard practice.

Faecal calprotectin
Faecal calprotectin is not the best initial test. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a well-recognised cause of erythema nodosum. Faecal calprotectin is a sensitive marker for intestinal inflammation and is used in the investigation of suspected IBD. However, in this patient who is described as being 'otherwise well with no other symptoms', there is no clinical suspicion of IBD. This investigation would be appropriate if the patient also reported abdominal pain, diarrhoea, or weight loss. As a screening test for allcomers with erythema nodosum, it has a much lower yield than a chest X-ray.

Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is not the most appropriate initial investigation. While serum ACE levels can be elevated in sarcoidosis, this test has significant limitations. It has poor sensitivity (elevated in only about 60% of cases) and specificity (can be elevated in other conditions like TB, diabetes, and liver disease). The chest X-ray is the primary screening tool for suspected pulmonary sarcoidosis, as the radiological findings, particularly bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, are far more diagnostic. Serum ACE is considered a second-line, supportive test rather than an initial screening investigation.

Skin biopsy
Skin biopsy is incorrect. Erythema nodosum is typically a clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic appearance and location of the tender nodules. A biopsy is generally not required and is reserved for atypical presentations where the diagnosis is uncertain. A biopsy would confirm septal panniculitis without vasculitis, which is the histological hallmark of erythema nodosum, but it would not provide any information about the underlying aetiology. The focus of investigation should be on identifying the systemic trigger, not on confirming the skin manifestation histologically.

stem: A 36-year-old dog walker presents with a skin rash. She describes intermittent flushing, worse on the days when she is at work. She also complains of bloating and diarrhoea, interspersed with constipation, for the past 10 years. There is no history of rectal bleeding, weight loss or fever. She would also like to discuss her low mood, which has been troubling her for the past year since the loss of her pet. On examination, you notice three erythematous papules with surrounding telangiectasia on the upper aspect of the cheek. The abdomen is soft with no tenderness or palpable masses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acne rosacea
Rosacea features: nose, cheeks and forehead flushing, erythema, telangiectasia → papules and pustules. This question highlights the importance of piecing information together and not merely reading keywords (such as 'flushing' and 'diarrhoea') and jumping to conclusions, a common way to get a question wrong in an exam. The intermittent flushing, which is worse on the days when she is at work, is likely to be due to photosensitivity as she works as a dog walker (outdoors). This, together with papules with telangiectasia, points to a diagnosis of acne rosacea. The aetiology of acne rosacea is not known. However, flushing is often the first symptom, and it is typically exacerbated by sunlight. The other symptoms are red herrings. Intermittent constipation and diarrhoea with bloating, especially with a normal examination and such a longstanding history, are likely due to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and unrelated to her skin rash. Low mood can exacerbate IBS symptoms and vice-versa. Patients will often present with several different symptoms, and they will often not know whether they are related or not. It is the clinician's job to determine whether they are relevant to the current presentation.

Allergic reaction
An allergic reaction is unlikely to manifest with flushing and papules with telangiectasia. It would typically cause hay fever-like symptoms or an urticarial erythematous rash, if not anaphylaxis.

Metastatic basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma of the skin can cause telangiectasia, but it is improbable that three of them would arise together on the same patch of skin or cause intermittent flushing.

Carcinoid syndrome
Carcinoid syndrome can entail flushing and diarrhoea and therefore is the main differential here. In carcinoid syndrome, the aforementioned symptoms usually indicate that a neuroendocrine tumour has metastasised to the liver and is releasing serotonin into the circulation. However, it wouldn't cause papules, and there are no red flags for cancer in this patient's history - she denied fever, bleeding or weight loss. It is very unlikely that several years' history of diarrhoea, particularly mixed with constipation, would be due to carcinoid syndrome having gone undiagnosed. Lastly, acne rosacea is much more common, statistically speaking, than carcinoid syndrome.

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia may cause telangiectasias but would also cause gastrointestinal and/or nosebleeds. The patient is having gastrointestinal symptoms. However, without any signs of bleeding, this is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

stem: A 37-year-old woman, currently 36 weeks pregnant with her second child, has developed an itchy rash on the lower third of her abdomen. She reports they initially appeared as small pink spots over her stretch marks. On examination, she has multiple large, erythematous plaques over her lower abdomen. Similar lesions also appear to be forming over her thighs. Her heart rate is 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 118/66 mmHg and she is afebrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy develops in the third trimester and is characterised by the development of pruritic papules, often over abdominal striae, that evolve into larger erythematous plaques and may also spread to the buttocks and thighs. Treatment would involve emollients and topical steroids. Consider oral steroids if particularly widespread.

Atopic eruption of pregnancy
Atopic eruption of pregnancy involves the development of a pruritic, eczematous rash, in the typical distribution seen in eczema. It is the most common skin problem in pregnancy, often presenting in the first or second trimester but may also present in the third. It often does not require specific treatment. The rash in this question does not have the eczematous distribution expected in the atopic eruption of pregnancy, and the evolution of pruritic papules to erythematous plaques is more characteristic of polymorphic eruption of pregnancy.

Bullous pemphigoid
Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune condition characterised by a tense blistering rash, most commonly seen in the elderly population. It can often be complicated by secondary bacterial or viral infection. The age, normal observations and lack of blistering make this very unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Pemphigoid gestationis
Pemphigoid gestationis is characterised by pruritic, blistering lesions, initially periumbilical but later spreading to affect the rest of the torso and arms over weeks. It is most often seen in the second or third trimester, or early postpartum, and in subsequent pregnancies may present sooner. Treatment would involve steroids but may require immunosuppression if severe. It is unlikely in this case due to the lack of blistering and distribution of lesions.

Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris is characterised by the formation of sometimes painful, fragile blisters, particularly on mucous membranes and may be complicated by secondary infection. Patients tend to be aged between 30-60 and it may be idiopathic, drug-induced, less commonly paraneoplastic or secondary to trauma or infection. Treat initially with systemic steroids.

stem: A 26-year-old man has returned from a beach holiday in Tenerife with a new rash on his neck and arms. On examination, there are patches which are coppery brown in colour and paler than the surrounding skin. There is no itch or pain associated with the rash. Examination with a Wood's light demonstrates yellow-green fluorescence in the affected areas. What is the first-line treatment of this skin condition?
explanation:
Ketoconazole shampoo
Ketoconazole shampoo is used to treat pityriasis versicolor. Pityriasis versicolor, also called tinea versicolor, is a superficial cutaneous fungal infection caused by Malassezia furfur. As in this case, it most commonly affects the trunk, neck and arms following a suntan. Generally, the rash is asymptomatic. UK guidelines recommend ketoconazole shampoo as first-line therapy. This question asks for first-line therapy and the description in the vignette is of limited, non-extensive disease.

Emollient
Emollient may help with any associated itch or irritation but is not sufficient in isolation to treat the fungal infection which underlies pityriasis versicolor.

Oral itraconazole
Oral antifungals, such as itraconazole, can be used when pityriasis versicolor is extensive or not responsive to topical treatment. This question asks for first-line therapy and the description in the vignette is of limited, non-extensive disease.

Topical steroids
Topical steroids may help with any associated itch or irritation but are not sufficient in isolation to treat the fungal infection which underlies pityriasis versicolor.

Vitamin D analogue
Topical vitamin D analogues, such as calcipotriol, are typically used to treat plaque psoriasis and do not have a role in the management of pityriasis versicolor.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and epilepsy presents with generalised increased hair growth over her trunk and arms. Which one of the following drugs is associated with hypertrichosis?
explanation:
Ciclosporin
The correct answer is Ciclosporin. Ciclosporin, an immunosuppressant drug used in the management of autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, can cause hypertrichosis as a side effect. Hypertrichosis, or excessive hair growth that is not androgen-dependent, has been reported in patients receiving ciclosporin therapy. This effect is thought to occur due to the drug's action on the hair cycle, prolonging the anagen phase (active growth phase) of hair follicles.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is an antiepileptic medication that can cause several side effects including weight gain, tremors and hair loss. Although it may cause changes in hair texture or even temporary alopecia, it is not associated with hypertrichosis.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone, a corticosteroid used in managing inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, also does not typically result in hypertrichosis. Its common side effects include weight gain, mood changes and osteoporosis among others.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin, another antiepileptic drug, can indeed cause changes in body hair including coarsening of hair and hirsutism (excessive growth of dark coarse hair in areas where women typically grow fine hair). However, phenytoin-induced hirsutism often presents as more localised to certain areas like the face and back rather than generalised over the body.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate, a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD), utilised for treating conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis does not generally lead to hypertrichosis. Instead, its side effects commonly involve gastrointestinal disturbances such as nausea and vomiting; haematological abnormalities like anaemia; or hepatotoxicity which necessitates regular liver function monitoring during treatment. Methotrexate might actually cause alopecia at high doses.

stem: A 54-year-old man attends the clinic with a rash. On examination, you note salmon-pink, thin, scaly, and ill-defined plaques in the skin folds on both sides of the face. What condition is associated with this skin disorder?
explanation:
HIV
HIV is associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis. This is a classic description of facial seborrhoeic dermatitis which is common in HIV-positive patients. Seborrheic dermatitis commonly affects areas of the skin with high sebum production, such as the scalp, nasolabial folds, glabella, eyebrows, beard, ears, retroauricular skin, sternum, and other skin folds. The facial rash typically presents with salmon-pink, thin, scaly, and ill-defined plaques in the nasolabial folds.

Alzheimer's disease
Alzheimer's disease is incorrect. It is Parkinson's disease (PD), rather than Alzheimer's disease which is associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis. Seborrhoeic dermatitis is considered to occur as a premotor feature of PD possibly due to dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. There is no association between multiple sclerosis and seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome is incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome can occur as a complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The malar rash of SLE typically occurs across the cheeks and nose but can include the forehead and chin. Importantly it spares the nasolabial folds in contrast to seborrhoeic dermatitis, making it a less likely diagnosis in this case.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. There is no association between rheumatoid arthritis and seborrhoeic dermatitis.

stem: A 25-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with a cough, sore throat and cold-like symptoms. He also reported the presence of a rash that was concerning him. Upon examination, there was a herald patch on his back with associated similar-looking smaller oval red patches that are located on his torso. What is the most likely cause of this rash?
explanation:
Human herpesvirus virus 7 (HHV-7)
Herpes hominis virus 7 (HHV-7) is thought to play a role in the aetiology of pityriasis rosea. Pityriasis rosea is associated with the reactivation of herpesviruses 6 and 7. The herald patch is a single plaque that appears 1-20 days prior to the generalised rash of pityriasis rosea.

Human herpesvirus virus 2 (HHV-2)
Human herpesvirus virus 2 (HHV-2) also commonly known as herpes simplex virus-2 (HSV-2) causes oral and/or genital herpes, therefore this is the incorrect answer in this case.

Human herpesvirus virus 3 (HHV-3)
Human herpesvirus virus 3 (HHV-3) also commonly known as varicellazoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox and shingles, therefore this is the incorrect answer in this case.

Human herpesvirus virus 4 (HHV-4)
Human herpesvirus virus 4 (HHV-4) also commonly known as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) causes Epstein-Barr virus-associated lymphoproliferative diseases, therefore this is the incorrect answer in this case.

Human herpesvirus virus 8 (HHV-8)
Human herpesvirus virus 8 (HHV-8) also commonly known as Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus causes Kaposi's sarcoma, therefore this is the incorrect answer in this case.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding scabies is false?
options: All members of the household should be treated
Typically affects the fingers, interdigital webs and flexor aspects of the wrist in adults
Scabies causes a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction
Patients who complain of pruritus 4 weeks following treatment should be retreated
Malathion is suitable for the eradication of scabies
explanation:
Patients who complain of pruritus 4 weeks following treatment should be retreated
The correct answer is 'Patients who complain of pruritus 4 weeks following treatment should be retreated'. This statement is false because itching can persist for up to 6 weeks after successful treatment due to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to the mites, even if all the mites have been killed. Retreatment should only be considered if new burrows or rashes appear, or if living mites are found upon examination.

All members of the household should be treated
All members of the household should be treated' - this statement is true. Scabies is highly contagious and can easily spread among people living in close quarters. Therefore, it's recommended that all members of a household, as well as any recent sexual partners, be treated at the same time to prevent re-infestation.

Typically affects the fingers, interdigital webs and flexor aspects of the wrist in adults
Typically affects the fingers, interdigital webs and flexor aspects of the wrist in adults' - this statement is also true. The Sarcoptes scabiei mite prefers warmer areas of the body such as these mentioned locations where they burrow into the skin and lay eggs.

Scabies causes a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction
Scabies causes a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction' - this statement is true as well. The intense itching associated with scabies isn't caused by the mites themselves but by an allergic reaction (type IV hypersensitivity) to their bodies, eggs and faeces.

Malathion is suitable for the eradication of scabies
Malathion is suitable for the eradication of scabies' - this statement is true too. Malathion 0.5% lotion (also known as Derbac-M) is indeed one of several treatments licensed in UK for use against scabies. It's particularly useful when first-line treatments cannot be used or have failed.

stem: Which one of the following complications is most associated with psoralen + ultraviolet A light (PUVA) therapy?
explanation:
Squamous cell cancer
The correct answer is Squamous cell cancer. PUVA therapy, which involves the use of psoralen (a photosensitizing medication) and ultraviolet A light, has been associated with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma. This is due to the mutagenic effect of UVA radiation on keratinocytes when used in conjunction with psoralen. The risk is particularly high in patients who have received a high cumulative dose of PUVA or those who have fair skin.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is not typically associated with PUVA therapy. Osteoporosis is primarily related to age, hormonal changes especially in post-menopausal women, low body mass index, smoking, excessive alcohol intake, and lack of physical activity among others. It's important to note that corticosteroids, which are sometimes used in the management of severe skin conditions like psoriasis, can lead to osteoporosis but this is not directly linked to PUVA therapy.

Basal cell cancer
Basal cell cancer, although it's a type of non-melanoma skin cancer like squamous cell carcinoma, is less frequently associated with PUVA compared to squamous cell carcinoma. Basal cell carcinomas are more commonly linked with chronic sun exposure and use of tanning beds.

Dermoid cysts
Dermoid cysts are benign tumours that often contain structures such as hair, fluid, teeth, or skin glands. They are most commonly found on the ovaries in women or near the lateral eyebrows in children. Dermoid cysts are not associated with PUVA therapy.

Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma, though a serious form of skin cancer, its association with PUVA therapy remains controversial and unclear. Some studies suggest a possible link while others don't. However, it's generally agreed that people receiving any form of phototherapy should be regularly screened for all types of skin cancers including malignant melanoma as part of good clinical practice.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with recurrent nosebleeds. He has no past medical history. His mother also suffered from recurrent nosebleeds. On examination, he has telangiectasia visible at the lips, hands and nose. Blood tests: Hb 101 g/L Male: (135-180) He undergoes a CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, which demonstrates a hepatic arteriovenous malformation. What is the inheritance pattern of the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia - autosomal dominant. Autosomal dominant is correct. This patient has a definite diagnosis of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia as evidenced by recurrent nosebleeds, telangiectases and an arteriovenous malformation (AVM). The inheritance pattern of this disorder is autosomal dominant. The recurrent nosebleeds affecting his mother suggests she also may have been affected.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. An example of a bleeding disorder (which can cause epistaxis) with this inheritance pattern is Bernard-Soulier syndrome. This is caused by a deficiency of the glycoprotein IbIX-V complex (GPIb-IX-V), the receptor for von Willebrand factor. Telangiectases and arteriovenous malformations (AVM) are not a feature of this condition so this is not the correct answer.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial is incorrect. Mitochondrial disorders are passed from mother to child as in this case. However, bleeding is not a common symptom of mitochondrial disorders, which typically have neurological manifestations such as strokes, dementia, myoclonus, and encephalopathy among others. This is therefore not correct.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect. Disorders characterized by an X-dominant pattern of inheritance are relatively uncommon. Examples include Fragile X and Rett syndromes. There is no X-linked dominant disorder that causes bleeding, telangiectasia, and hepatic AVMs and this is therefore incorrect.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. This is the inheritance pattern of haemophilia A. This occurs almost exclusively in males due to its X-linked recessive inheritance pattern (as males only have one X chromosome). It can of course cause nosebleeds due to a genetic deficiency in clotting factor VIII. However, as with the other options, telangiectases and arteriovenous malformations (AVM) are not a feature of this condition so this is not the correct answer.

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends the GP with a rash. She has a bright red rash over her nose and cheeks. She reports that drinking alcohol makes her rash worse and this is really embarrassing for her. She reports occasional pustules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acne rosacea
Rosacea features: nose, cheeks and forehead flushing, erythema, telangiectasia → papules and pustules. This is a typical history of acne rosacea. Pustules point towards acne, and the erythematous nature of the rash suggests this is rosacea. Rosacea generally worsens with alcohol.

Acne vulgaris
In acne vulgaris, you would expect to see comedones, papules, pustules, nodules, and/or cysts. It is generally less erythematous than rosacea.

Erythema ab igne
Erythema ab igne is an erythematous rash caused by high levels of heat or infra-red radiation. Often you will see this being caused by hot water bottles or radiators.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis typically presents with a silver-scale rash. It is an immunemediated rash that typically presents on extensor surfaces (knees & elbows).

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Although this description could fit with a butterfly rash, there is nothing in the history to suggest lupus.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is reviewed in the dermatology clinic with patchy, well demarcated hair loss on the scalp. This is affecting around 20% of her total scalp, and causing significant psychological distress. A diagnosis of alopecia areata is suspected. Which one of the following is an appropriate management plan?
explanation:
Topical corticosteroid
Topical corticosteroid is an appropriate management plan for alopecia areata. Watchful waiting for spontaneous remission is another option.

Autoimmune screen
The British Association of Dermatologists does not recommend screening for autoimmune disease.

Autoimmune screen + topical ketoconazole
The British Association of Dermatologists does not recommend screening for autoimmune disease.

stem: A 72-year-old woman attends dermatology clinic with a skin change on her lower back that has developed over several months. She has chronic lower back pain managed with paracetamol. Examination reveals a reticulated, hyperpigmented patch with overlying telangiectasia in the lumbar region. What is the most important advice to give?
explanation:
Avoid further heat exposure
Erythema ab igne is caused by infrared radiation and is commonly associated with hot water bottles or open fires. Avoid further heat exposure is the most important advice. This patient has erythema ab igne, a reticulated hyperpigmented rash caused by chronic infrared radiation exposure. The lumbar distribution in someone with chronic back pain strongly suggests use of a heat source such as a hot water bottle or heating pad for pain relief. The key management principle is removing the heat source to prevent progression. Continued exposure can lead to epidermal atrophy and, importantly, an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma developing within the affected area. While the existing pigmentation may fade partially over months to years after cessation of heat exposure, preventing malignant transformation is the primary concern.

Apply emollient twice daily
Apply emollient twice daily may provide symptomatic relief for any associated dryness but does not address the underlying cause. Emollients will not prevent disease progression or the risk of malignancy if heat exposure continues.

Start topical corticosteroid
Start topical corticosteroid is not indicated as this is not an inflammatory dermatosis. Corticosteroids would not treat the underlying thermal injury and may cause skin atrophy with prolonged use.

Commence oral antihistamine
Commence oral antihistamine would be appropriate for pruritic conditions but erythema ab igne is typically asymptomatic and not histamine-mediated.

Use high-factor sunscreen
Use high-factor sunscreen is general advice for hyperpigmented skin but does not address the causative heat exposure in this thermal injury.

stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis comes for review. Six years ago he had an ileostomy formed which has been functioning well until now. Unfortunately he is currently suffering significant pain around the stoma site. On examination a deep erythematous ulcer is noted with a ragged edge. The surrounding skin is erythematous and swollen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is associated with inflammatory bowel disease and may be seen around the stoma site. Treatment is usually with immunosuppressants as surgery may worsen the problem. A differential diagnosis would be malignancy and hence lesions should be referred for specialist opinion to evaluate the need for a biopsy.

Irritant contact dermatitis
Irritant contact dermatitis is common but would not be expected to cause such a deep ulcer.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with excessive hair growth on her face. She has a past medical history of obesity and her body mass index is 35 kg/m². On examination, she has thick dark hair on her face. After trialling weight loss, what pharmacological treatment is most appropriate?
explanation:
Eflornithine
Topical eflornithine is the treatment of choice for facial hirsutism. The patient has thick dark hair on her face, which is consistent with facial hirsutism. It is likely that obesity is the cause in this case. Topical eflornithine is a treatment for facial hirsutism and when applied to the skin works by blocking the action of an enzyme in hair follicles that causes hair growth.

Corticosteroids
Corticosteroids is incorrect. This condition would both worsen her obesity and may actually cause rather than treat hirsutism.

Diazoxide
Diazoxide is incorrect. This is used in the management of hypoglycaemia in those patients who use too much insulin. Rather than treating hirsutism, it causes hypertrichosis (which is androgen-independent hair growth).

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. This may be effective in treating hirsutism in patients with polycystic ovary syndrome, which is not present in this case. In those patients with hirsutism limited to the face, topical eflornithine is a more appropriate choice.

Minoxidil
Minoxidil is incorrect. This is actually used to stimulate hair growth in men and women with hair loss.

stem: A 16-year-old man presents to the department with a rapidly progressive painful rash affecting his face, torso, abdomen, back, and all 4 limbs. He has a past medical history of atopic dermatitis. On examination, you note a generalised monomorphic blistering rash, some of which have ruptured to release a clear yellow fluid. Some of the blisters have central dimples. A 5cm by 6cm patch over the chest contains pustules and honey-coloured crusted erosions. What treatment is urgently required?
explanation:
Aciclovir
Eczema herpeticum is a serious condition that requires IV antivirals. Aciclovir is correct. This is a classic description of eczema herpeticum which is a disseminated viral infection characterised by fever and clusters of itchy blisters or punched-out erosions. It is most often seen as a complication of atopic dermatitis/eczema. Most cases of eczema herpeticum are due to herpes simplex type 1 or 2. It is a dermatological emergency and requires prompt treatment with an anti-viral such as aciclovir or valacyclovir.

Amphotericin B
Amphotericin B is incorrect. Amphotericin B is an antifungal medication used to treat mucormycosis, aspergillosis, blastomycosis, candidiasis, coccidioidomycosis, and cryptococcosis. The clinical examination does not support any of the aforementioned conditions.

Cidofovir
Cidofovir is incorrect. Cidofovir is an antiviral that can be used in aciclovir-resistant herpes simplex infections. If the infection did not respond to aciclovir then sensitivity testing could be performed to assess for resistance.

Flucloxacillin
Flucloxacillin is incorrect. Although the patient may well have a secondary bacterial infection (e.g. impetigo on their chest), the most important part of treatment is prompt initiation of an anti-viral. The addition of flucloxacillin to cover for a superadded Staphylococcus aureus infection would be reasonable.

Vancomycin
Vancomycin is incorrect. If the patient were to have a confirmed or suspected methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), then it would be reasonable to initiate them on vancomycin in addition to aciclovir to cover for superadded bacterial infection.

stem: A 54-year-old man who is known to have gastric cancer is reviewed in clinic. He asks you about a rash he has developed. Which of the following skin disorders is most associated with gastric cancer?
explanation:
Acanthosis nigricans
The correct answer is acanthosis nigricans. Acanthosis nigricans is a skin disorder characterised by hyperpigmentation and 'velvety' thickening of the skin, especially in body folds such as the armpits and neck. It is most commonly associated with insulin resistance (as seen in type 2 diabetes) but can also be a paraneoplastic syndrome, associated with gastric adenocarcinoma among other malignancies.

Erythema gyratum repens
Erythema gyratum repens is a very rare paraneoplastic dermatosis characterised by concentric, erythematous bands that migrate across the skin surface. It has been linked to lung cancer more frequently than any other malignancy, but it's not typically associated with gastric cancer.

Necrolytic migratory erythema
Necrolytic migratory erythema is another paraneoplastic syndrome often associated with glucagonoma, a tumour of the pancreas. The rash usually presents as red, swollen and blistering or crusted patches on the skin that then spread outwards. It is not particularly linked to gastric cancer.

Sweet's syndrome
Sweet's syndrome, or acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, presents as painful plaques on the head, neck and arms along with fever and leukocytosis. It can be associated with various conditions including infections, inflammatory diseases and malignancies such as leukemia but it's not particularly linked to gastric cancer.

Acquired ichthyosis
Acquired ichthyosis is a disorder of keratinisation leading to dry, scaly skin resembling fish scales. It can be idiopathic or associated with systemic diseases like lymphoma or HIV infection; however, it does not have a strong association with gastric cancer.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is referred to psychiatry following repeated episodes of hypomaniac behaviour interspersed with periods of depression. Her past medical history includes psoriasis and a deep vein thrombosis 11 years ago. Which one of the following medications is most likely to worsen her psoriasis?
explanation:
Lithium
Lithium is known to exacerbate psoriasis in some patients. The exact mechanism by which lithium worsens psoriasis is not completely understood, but it is thought to be related to its effects on the immune system and skin cell proliferation. Lithium can cause an increase in the production of certain cytokines that play a role in the development of psoriasis, as well as directly stimulate keratinocyte proliferation.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate and Valproaic acid (which are essentially the same medication) are anticonvulsant medications that can also be used as mood stabilisers for patients with bipolar disorder. While they do have some immunomodulatory effects, there is no strong evidence to suggest that they significantly exacerbate psoriasis. In fact, some studies have suggested that valproate may even have a beneficial effect on psoriasis due to its anti-inflammatory properties.

Quetiapine
Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic medication that can also be used as a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder. There have been isolated case reports of quetiapine-induced psoriasis; however, these are rare occurrences and not considered a common side effect of the medication. Overall, quetiapine is less likely than lithium to worsen psoriasis.

Valproaic acid
Sodium valproate and Valproaic acid (which are essentially the same medication) are anticonvulsant medications that can also be used as mood stabilisers for patients with bipolar disorder. While they do have some immunomodulatory effects, there is no strong evidence to suggest that they significantly exacerbate psoriasis. In fact, some studies have suggested that valproate may even have a beneficial effect on psoriasis due to its anti-inflammatory properties.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant medication. Although SSRIs can potentially cause various skin reactions, including rash and pruritus, there is no consistent evidence linking fluoxetine specifically with the worsening of psoriasis.

stem: A 69-year-old male presents with a non-healing ulcer at the site of a flame burn injury on his foot 8 years ago. The burn injury was managed with dressings and skin grafting but has never healed completely. Over the last 3 months, he has suffered from recurrent bleeding and ulceration at this site. On examination, there is extensive scarring on the dorsal aspect of his foot there is a 30mm ulcerated area with associated tenderness. Histopathology report confirmed malignant disease describing the presence of keratin pearls. Imaging showed evidence of metastases. Which of the following is the most likely malignancy?
explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
SCCs arising in a chronic scar are typically more aggressive and carry an increased risk of metastasis. A history of a non-healing ulcer at the site of a burn injury should be investigated immediately for SCC. Squamous cell carcinomas arising in chronic wounds tend to be more aggressive so early diagnosis and biopsy are important to prevent metastatic disease. They can also be seen in other chronic wounded, scarred or inflamed skin e.g. skin overlying focus of osteomyelitis, scars, radiotherapy scars and venous ulcers.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)
A literature review of 412 cases of malignancy at burn wound sites found that 293 (71%) were SCCs, 48 (12%) were BCCs, 23 (6%) were melanomas, 21 (5%) were sarcomas, and the remaining were other neoplasms. Basal cell carcinomas are less common in burn scars and are generally less aggressive.

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma appears as scaly pruritic patches or plaques. It would not arise in a scar, wound, or burn.

Melanoma
A literature review of 412 cases of malignancy at burn wound sites found that 293 (71%) were SCCs, 48 (12%) were BCCs, 23 (6%) were melanomas, 21 (5%) were sarcomas, and the remaining were other neoplasms. Melanomas are less common in burn scars.

Sarcoma
A literature review of 412 cases of malignancy at burn wound sites found that 293 (71%) were SCCs, 48 (12%) were BCCs, 23 (6%) were melanomas, 21 (5%) were sarcomas, and the remaining were other neoplasms. Sarcomas are less common in burn scars.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is seen in the GP clinic. She complains of a rash predominantly over her cheeks and nose which is worse in sunlight and if she drinks alcohol. It has started over the last 1 year. On examination, she has erythematous, raised cheeks with uneven texture, widespread telangiectasia and severe inflammatory pustules. Despite having already taken measures to wear sun-cream and avoid alcohol, she feels the rash is worsening and is now permanent. What regimen should the GP prescribe as first-line treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Topical ivermectin and oral doxycycline
Rosacea: a combination of topical ivermectin + oral doxycycline is first-line for patients with severe papules and/or pustules. The condition being described is rosacea. It is a chronic skin condition typically affecting women aged 30-60 years. Early features include flushing and telangiectasia of the nose, cheeks and forehead; for some people, this develops into persistent erythema with papules and pustules, as in this case. Common triggers which exacerbate symptoms include sunlight, spicy foods, alcohol, caffeine and stress. In this case, the patient has erythema and severe pustules. The recommended first-line treatment for severe pustular disease in rosacea is topical ivermectin and oral doxycycline so this is the correct answer.

Topical brimonidine
Topical brimonidine can be used for patients with predominant flushing but limited telangiectasia. This is not appropriate in this case since her erythema is persistent and she has severe pustules.

Topical hydrocortisone
Topical hydrocortisone is not used in the management of rosacea.

Topical ivermectin
For mild-moderate pustular disease, topical ivermectin monotherapy is recommended. However, given the severe pustules in this case, this is an incorrect answer.

Topical metronidazole
Topical metronidazole can also be used as an alternative to topical ivermectin in mild-moderate disease. As above, this answer is incorrect in this question because the patient has severe pustules.

stem: A 45-year-old man who presented with itchy lesions on his hands is diagnosed with scabies. It is decided to treat him with permethrin 5%. You have explained the need to treat all members of the household and hot wash all bedding and clothes. What advice should be given about applying the cream?
options: From neck down + leave for 12 hours
All skin including scalp + leave for 12 hours + repeat in 2 days
All skin including scalp + leave for 12 hours + repeat in 7 days
From neck down + leave for 4 hours
From neck down + leave for 12 hours + repeat in 7 days
explanation:
All skin including scalp + leave for 12 hours + repeat in 7 days
Scabies - permethrin treatment: all skin including scalp + leave for 12 hours + retreat in 7 days The BNF advises to apply the insecticide to all areas, including the face and scalp, contrary to the manufacturer's recommendation (and common practice).

From neck down + leave for 12 hours
This option only treats from the neck down and does not include the scalp, which is not sufficient according to the BNF guidelines.

All skin including scalp + leave for 12 hours + repeat in 2 days
This option suggests repeating the treatment in 2 days, but the correct interval is 7 days according to the BNF guidelines.

From neck down + leave for 4 hours
This option only treats from the neck down and leaves the cream on for 4 hours, which is not sufficient according to the BNF guidelines.

From neck down + leave for 12 hours + repeat in 7 days
This option only treats from the neck down and does not include the scalp, which is not sufficient according to the BNF guidelines.

stem: A 34-year-old female is reviewed in the dermatology clinic with a skin rash under her new wrist watch. An allergy to nickel is suspected. What is the best investigation?
explanation:
Skin patch test
The correct answer is Skin patch test. Skin patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosing contact dermatitis, such as nickel allergy. It involves applying a small amount of various substances, including nickel, to the skin using adhesive patches. The patches are usually left on for 48 hours and then removed. The skin is then examined for signs of an allergic reaction.

Skin prick test
Skin prick tests are typically used to diagnose IgE-mediated allergies, such as food or pollen allergies. They involve pricking the skin with a needle or lancet that contains a small amount of a suspected allergen. A positive result appears as a wheal (a raised, red bump) at the site of testing within 15-20 minutes. However, this method isn't suitable for diagnosing contact dermatitis because these reactions are not IgE-mediated.

Skin biopsy
While it can be useful in diagnosing some types of skin conditions like psoriasis or skin cancer, it's generally not necessary for diagnosing contact dermatitis unless there's uncertainty about the diagnosis or if other diseases need to be ruled out.

Serum IgE
Serum IgE levels are often measured when an IgE-mediated allergy is suspected, such as asthma or atopic dermatitis. Elevated levels of serum IgE may indicate an allergic response but do not provide specific information about what substance the person is allergic to and therefore would not be helpful in diagnosing a nickel allergy.

Serum nickel antibodies
Measuring Serum nickel antibodies is not routinely done in clinical practice due to a lack of specificity and sensitivity in detecting contact dermatitis caused by nickel exposure. This makes it an unreliable test for diagnosing nickel allergy.

stem: A 74-year-old lady with a history of hypothyroidism presents in January with a rash down the right side of her body. On examination an erythematous rash with patches of hyperpigmentation and telangiectasia is found. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema ab igne
Erythema ab igne is caused by infrared radiation and is commonly associated with hot water bottles or open fires. This is a classic presentation of erythema ab igne.

Pretibial myxoedema
Despite the name, pretibial myxoedema is associated with hyperthyroidism rather than hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism can make patients feel cold and hence more likely to sit next to a heater / fire.

stem: A 53-year-old man presents to his GP with a skin lesion on his lower left leg. He describes an increasing size nodule below his left knee overlying a previous burn scar he acquired 20 years ago in a house fire. He first noticed this about 3 weeks ago. He is normally fit and well and takes no other medications. He does however smoke 20 cigarettes a day. On examination, there is a non-tender 3x3cm nodule with some developing ulceration overlying a large thermal burn scar below the left knee. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
A non-healing painless ulcer associated with a chronic scar is indicative of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). This man has two risk factors for developing an SCC; a previous thermal injury and smoking. A nodule which develops into a non-healing ulcer over weeks to months is typical for SCC. These lesions may be painless and may bleed.

Actinic keratosis
Actinic keratoses are pre-malignant lesions which appear on sun-exposed areas. They tend to appear warty or scaly but do not ulcerate unless they progress to SCC. There is an association with sun exposure but not with thermal burn scars.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)
This scenario could also represent a BCC which develops on sun-exposed skin and over a previous area of a thermal burn injury. They also tend to ulcerate. However, BCCs grow more slowly and tend to be described as a pearly nodule with a central depression or a rolled border. You would therefore not expect the lesion described to have developed to this size within 3 weeks if it was a BCC.

Diabetic ulcer
Diabetic ulcers tend to affect the feet initially and result from neurovascular compromise resulting from poorly controlled or longstanding diabetes. There are no features to suggest that this man may be diabetic, such as polyuria or polydipsia, and there is no suggestion that there is any sensory loss or vascular compromise.

Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma results from the cancerous growth of melanocytes. The first sign is normally an unusual-looking freckle or mole that becomes itchy, irregular or bleeds. As they progress they tend to become thickened and raised but they rarely ulcerate. There is a strong association with sun exposure and sunburn but not with thermal burn scars.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding acne vulgaris is incorrect?
options: Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation results in obstruction of the pilosebaceous follicle
Acne vulgaris affects at least 80% of teenagers
Propionibacterium acnes is an anaerobic bacterium
Typical lesions include comedones and pustules
Beyond the age of 25 years acne vulgaris is more common in males
explanation:
Beyond the age of 25 years acne vulgaris is more common in males
Beyond the age of 25 years acne vulgaris is more common in males is incorrect. In fact, postadolescent acne is more common in females, affecting approximately 12-14% of women compared to 3% of men over age 25. This gender disparity is thought to be due to hormonal influences, particularly the role of androgens and their effect on sebum production.

Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation results in obstruction of the pilosebaceous follicle
Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation results in obstruction of the pilosebaceous follicle is correct. This is one of the four key pathophysiological factors in acne development. The hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation of keratinocytes leads to microcomedone formation, which is the precursor of all acne lesions.

Acne vulgaris affects at least 80% of teenagers
Acne vulgaris affects at least 80% of teenagers is correct. Studies consistently show that approximately 80-90% of adolescents in Western populations experience acne to some degree during their teenage years, making it one of the most common dermatological conditions in this age group.

Propionibacterium acnes is an anaerobic bacterium
Propionibacterium acnes is an anaerobic bacterium is correct. Now also known as *Cutibacterium acnes*, this gram-positive anaerobic bacterium is a normal component of skin flora that proliferates in the lipid-rich environment of the pilosebaceous unit. It contributes to inflammation in acne through various mechanisms including the production of inflammatory mediators.

Typical lesions include comedones and pustules
Typical lesions include comedones and pustules is correct. The clinical manifestations of acne include non-inflammatory lesions (open and closed comedones) and inflammatory lesions (papules, pustules, and nodules). Comedones and pustules are indeed characteristic features of acne vulgaris.

stem: A 28-year-old car mechanic presented with symptoms of itchy blisters on his palms, fingers and soles of his feet. Over the past few days, they have become intensely itchy to the point where he struggles to sleep at night. He reports that his work has become very stressful recently and the summer heat means he is sweating more too. What is the most likely skin condition in this case?
explanation:
Pompholyx eczema
Pompholyx eczema may be precipitated by humidity (e.g. sweating) and high temperatures. Pompholyx (also known as dyshidrotic eczema) is a type of eczema which causes tiny blisters to arise across the fingers, palms of the hands and in some cases the soles of the feet. It commonly affects adults under 40 years old. The exact causes of pompholyx eczema are unknown, but factors such as stress, sensitivity to metal compounds e.g. nickel or cobalt, sweating can aggravate it.

Discoid eczema
Discoid eczema is a common type of eczema/dermatitis defined by scattered, well-defined, coin-shaped and coin-sized plaques of eczema. Blisters occur less commonly meaning it is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Palmoplantar hyperhidrosis
Palmoplantar hyperhidrosis is a common condition in which sweat glands of the palms and soles produce inappropriately large quantities of sweat, worse in warmer weather. Blisters occur less commonly meaning it is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Palmoplantar keratoderma
Palmoplantar keratoderma is a skin condition characterised by thickening of the skin on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, which is not described here.

Palmoplantar pustulosis
Palmoplantar pustulosis is an autoimmune disorder marked by the appearance of fluid-filled pustules or blisters on the hands and feet and is considered to be a variant of psoriasis. The pustules may be painful and cause a burning feeling, which is not the case here.

stem: A 38-year-old man is referred to the dermatology outpatient department with a recurrent rash on his face and dorsal hands, which seems to be precipitated by occasional alcohol use and sun exposure. He has no past medical history. On examination, a blistering rash was noted on his face and dorsal hands. Diffuse excessive hair growth is noted throughout his body. Blood tests are performed. Hb 136 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 189 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 4.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Hepatitis C antibodies negative What is the underlying mechanism that explains his symptoms?
options: Mutations in the gene that encodes Δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase
explanation:
Inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Porphyria cutanea tarda is caused by an inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. The patient presents with a blistering rash on the face and dorsal hands provoked by sunlight and alcohol. In addition, there is hypertrichosis (excessive hair growth in non-androgen-dependent areas of the body). These findings suggest a diagnosis of porphyria cutanea tarda. This can be inherited or acquired due to hepatocyte damage (i.e. hepatitis C infection or alcohol excess). In the setting of negative testing for hepatitis C and the absence of alcohol excess, this is likely due to an inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

Hepatocyte damage
Hepatitis C is a common cause of porphyria cutanea tarda and serology should always be checked in suspected cases. In the setting of negative testing for hepatitis C and the absence of alcohol excess, this is likely due to an inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

Inhibition of Δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD)
Inhibition of Δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) is incorrect. This is another defect in the haem metabolism pathway and is the main mechanism by which lead poisoning causes iron deficiency. The patient is not anaemic and there is no suggestion of lead poisoning, which does not cause this type of blistering rash or hypertrichosis.

Mutations in porphobilinogen deaminase
Mutations in porphobilinogen deaminase is incorrect. This is another defect in the haem metabolism pathway, resulting in acute intermittent porphyria. Recurrent attacks of abdominal pain and neurological dysfunction including peripheral neuropathy and seizures characterise this. These features are not present here and so it is PCT rather than AIP that is the likely disorder.

Mutations in the gene that encodes Δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase
