Pemphigus vulgaris, the most common type, often starts with mouth sores followed by skin blisters. However, these blisters are flaccid and easily rupture unlike those seen in pompholyx or bullous pemphigoid.

stem: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 0, presents to the fertility clinic. All 4 of her pregnancies resulted in spontaneous abortion after the 10th week of pregnancy. She also describes joint pain, discolouration of the fingers of both hands in cold weather and macular rashes. The patient is sexually active and taking a daily prenatal multivitamin. There is bilateral polyarthropathy with effusion affecting fingers, toes, and knees. There's an ulcer on the left middle finger. You also note alopecia and purple reticular rash on both calves. What is the most specific test for the underlying condition?
explanation:
Anti-Smith antibody
The most specific tests for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) antibody and an anti-Smith (Sm) antibody with 99% specificity. In this scenario, SLE is the underlying disease, and the most specific test is the anti-Smith antibody.

Anti-centromere antibody
Anti-centromere antibodies are strongly associated with CREST syndrome (calcinosis cutis, Raynaud phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia). Skin involvement is a defining feature of CREST syndrome, and includes thickening and hardening with redness and oedematous swelling. This is not provided with this patient.

Anti-histone antibody
Anti-histone antibodies are present in more than 95% of patients with drug-induced lupus, especially among those taking procainamide, hydralazine, chlorpromazine, and quinidine. There is no such drug history in this patient.

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MP), and other autoimmune vasculitides. Though GPA and MP can lead to cutaneous ulceration, lack of upper respiratory tract (such as sinusitis), lower respiratory tract and renal involvement make them unlikely.

Anti-nuclear antibody
Due to its high sensitivity, anti-nuclear antibodies are present virtually in all patients with SLE. But it is a nonspecific marker as this is associated with several rheumatological autoimmune conditions.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency room with a blistering rash on the backs of her hands and face. She has recently returned from a family holiday in Egypt. She reports that her father has experienced similar rashes previously. A urine sample reveals elevated levels of uroporphyrins. What is the defective enzyme associated with the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
The correct answer is a defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, leading to the presentation of porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT). Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase converts uroporphyrinogen III into coproporphyrinogen III, one of the many reactions in synthesizing heme. The patient has a new blistering rash on sun-exposed areas of the body after a holiday to a country with a hot climate, implying photosensitivity. Given the familial history and raised urinary uroporphyrinogen, the most likely diagnosis is PCT. PCT classically presents with a photosensitive, fragile and blistering rash on the face and dorsal aspects of the hands. Hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation may also be present. Patients will have a raised uroporphyrinogen and pink fluorescence of the urine when viewed under Wood's lamp.

Aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALA synthase)
ALA synthase converts glycine and succinyl-CoA to delta-aminolevulinic acid. It is disrupted in X-linked sideroblastic anaemia.

Porphobilinogen deaminase
Porphobilinogen deaminase converts porphobilinogen into hydroxymethylbilane and is defective in acute intermittent porphyria.

Porphobilinogen synthase
Porphobilinogen synthase is responsible for the conversion of delta-aminolevulinic acid into porphobilinogen and is disrupted in lead poisoning. It is also known as ALA dehydratase.

Protoporphyrin ferrochelatase
Protoporphyrin ferrochelatase is responsible for the conversion of protoporphyrin into haem and is also defective in lead poisoning. It is implicated more in the development of erythropoietic protoporphyria.

stem: A 14-year-old male is reviewed due to a patch of scaling and hair loss on the right side of his head. A skin scraping is sent which confirms a diagnosis of tinea capitis. Which organism is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Trichophyton tonsurans
The correct answer is Trichophyton tonsurans. Tinea capitis, a dermatophyte infection of the scalp, is most commonly caused by Trichophyton tonsurans in the UK. The fungus invades the hair shaft leading to scaling and hair loss. Treatment involves systemic antifungal therapy as topical treatments do not penetrate the hair shaft.

Microsporum distortum
Microsporum distortum is an incorrect answer. This organism is a rare cause of tinea infections and when involved, it typically causes tinea corporis (ringworm) rather than tinea capitis.

Trichophyton verrucosum
Trichophyton verrucosum is another incorrect choice. This organism primarily affects cattle and can cause tinea corporis in humans through direct contact with infected animals or contaminated soil but it rarely causes tinea capitis.

Microsporum audouinii
The option Microsporum audouinii, although incorrect, was once a common cause of tinea capitis in Europe but now its incidence has significantly decreased due to improved hygiene and living conditions. It's worth noting that Microsporum species usually fluoresce under Wood's lamp examination which can be helpful in diagnosis.

Microsporum canis
Microsporum canis, also an incorrect option, primarily affects cats and dogs and may cause tinea capitis in humans through direct contact with infected pets. However, it's less common compared to Trichophyton tonsurans, especially in the urban settings where pet ownership is less common.

stem: Which of the following conditions is least likely to exhibit the Koebner phenomenon?
explanation:
Lupus vulgaris
Lupus vulgaris is not associated with the Koebner phenomenon.

stem: A 34-year-old man with a history of polyarthralgia, back pain and diarrhoea is found to have a 3 cm red lesion on his shin which is starting to ulcerate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyoderma gangrenosum
This patient is likely to have ulcerative colitis, which has a known association with large-joint arthritis, sacroilitis and pyoderma gangrenosum.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with multiple erythematous target lesions two days after starting a new medication. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to have been started?
explanation:
Carbamazepine
This patient appears to have erythema multiforme which is a known complication of carbamazepine use.

stem: A 62-year-old female is referred to dermatology due to a lesion over her shin. It initially started as a small red papule which later became a deep, red, necrotic ulcer with a violaceous border. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyoderma gangrenosum
This is a classic description of pyoderma gangrenosum.

stem: A 62-year-old woman mentions in diabetes clinic that she has a 'volcano' like spot on her left cheek, which has appeared over the past 3 months. She initially thought it may be a simple spot but it has not gone away. On examination she has a 5 mm red, raised lesion with a central keratin filled crater. A clinical diagnosis of probable keratoacanthoma is made. What is the most suitable management?
options: Reassure will spontaneously involute within 3 months
explanation:
Urgent referral to dermatology
Whilst keratoacanthoma is a benign lesion it is difficult clinically to exclude squamous cell carcinoma so urgent excision is advised.

stem: A 17-year-old male is reviewed six weeks after starting an oral antibiotic for acne vulgaris. He stopped taking the drug two weeks ago due to perceived alteration in his skin colour, and denies been exposed to strong sunlight for the past six months. On examination he has generalised increased skin pigmentation, including around the buttocks. Which one of the following antibiotics was he likely to be taking?
explanation:
Minocycline
Minocycline can cause irreversible skin pigmentation and is now considered a second line drug in acne.

Doxycycline
Photosensitivity secondary to tetracycline/doxycycline is less likely given the generalised distribution of the pigmentation and the failure to improve following drug withdrawal

Tetracycline
Photosensitivity secondary to tetracycline/doxycycline is less likely given the generalised distribution of the pigmentation and the failure to improve following drug withdrawal.

stem: Which of the following conditions is most associated with onycholysis?
explanation:
Raynaud's disease
Raynaud's disease causes onycholysis, as can any cause of impaired circulation.

stem: A 49-year-old man is reviewed in the dermatology clinic complaining of losing hair. Examination reveals generalised scalp hair loss that does not follow the typical male-pattern distribution. Which one of the following medications is least likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Phenytoin
Phenytoin is a recognised cause of hirsutism, rather than alopecia.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to dermatology clinic with an itchy rash on his palms. He has also noticed the rash around the site of a recent scar on his forearm. Examination reveals papules with a white-lace pattern on the surface. Some isolated white streaks are also noted on the mucous membranes of the mouth. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen planus
Lichen planus: purple, pruritic, papular, polygonal rash on flexor surfaces. Wickham's striae over surface. Oral involvement common

Lichen sclerosus
Lichen sclerosus: itchy white spots typically seen on the vulva of elderly women.

stem: A 26-year-old man who is HIV positive is noted to have developed seborrhoeic dermatitis. Which of the following two complications are most associated with this condition?
explanation:
Blepharitis and otitis externa
Otitis externa and blepharitis are common complications of seborrhoeic dermatitis

Alopecia and otitis externa
Alopecia is not commonly seen in seborrhoeic dermatitis, but may develop if a severe secondary infection develops

Photosensitivity and alopecia
Alopecia is not commonly seen in seborrhoeic dermatitis, but may develop if a severe secondary infection develops

Photosensitivity and blepharitis
Alopecia is not commonly seen in seborrhoeic dermatitis, but may develop if a severe secondary infection develops

Blepharitis and alopecia
Alopecia is not commonly seen in seborrhoeic dermatitis, but may develop if a severe secondary infection develops.
